Assuming the data follows a mixture model, we establish a spectral analysis of the neural tangent kernel and derive a bound for the generalization error. Our findings indicate that generalization performance degrades when training on one distribution and evaluating on another, a phenomenon explained by an analysis of the eigenfunctions and eigenvalues of the neural tangent kernel. Additionally, we present a bound for random features algorithms that is nearly as tight as one describing the generalization error of random features. This bound reveals a critical relationship between the generalization error of neural tangent kernels and classical random features algorithms. Finally, numerical experiments demonstrate the efficacy of our spectral analysis and error bounds across various scenarios. These results are detailed in a paper submitted to the Information Theory Workshop (ITW) in 2021.

a promising approach for developing robotic control strategies. However, applying RL to novel or unseen environments remains challenging due to the high sample complexity required to gather sufficient data. This difficulty is particularly evident in tasks involving contact dynamics, such as walking, where the precise timing and magnitude of contact forces are critical. Current RL-based walking controllers often require extensive trial-and-error to learn effective policies, a process that is impractical in real-world settings due to its time-consuming nature. Consequently, there is an urgent need to accelerate the learning of control policies. To address this, we introduce a prior-guided RL framework designed to enhance sample efficiency for tasks characterized by contact dynamics. Our approach utilizes a dynamics model to forecast the effects of candidate control actions, thereby directing the collection of samples in the physical environment to maximize information gain. We implemented this framework on a legged robot tasked with walking across a variety of terrains. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves efficient walking behavior by learning a policy with significantly fewer samples compared to a standard RL baseline. Furthermore, we validated the framework's generalizability by testing it on multiple tasks and different dynamics models, including both linear and nonlinear controllers as well as muscle actuators. Across all variations, our prior-guided framework consistently outperformed the baseline in sample efficiency. The source code can be accessed at https://github.com/ashishbhat/PGRL. This work was previously presented at the 2021 IEEE/RSJ International Conference on Intelligent Robots and Systems (IROS).

deteriorates over time due to the degradation of controlled components. To address this, we introduce a degradation-aware optimal control framework designed to maximize average performance. This model incorporates a stochastic degradation process that influences plant behavior, with the controller dynamically adjusting actions to uphold a specified minimum distribution for the degradation level. Furthermore, the optimal control policy is derived to minimize the financial costs associated with both energy consumption and equipment maintenance. Using a piecewise linear approximation of the degradation process enables the formulation of this problem as a pair of coupled coupled Bellman equations, solvable via value iteration. The resulting controller is implemented as a feedback law that maps the current state to the appropriate action. A numerical example utilizing a Brownian motion model for the plant demonstrates the synthesis of this controller and validates the significant improvements in both cost efficiency and performance. This methodology is broadly applicable to any system featuring a continuous stochastic process, such as those found in chemical, biological, and mechanical domains. The developed approach holds particular promise for managing aging systems within the manufacturing sector. Furthermore, the methodology is extensible to scenarios involving multiple energy sources, specific equipment maintenance strategies, and situations where the degradation level directly impacts performance. The code necessary to replicate the numerical example is accessible at https://github.com/CSHLAB/DAOC.

stars within the Milky Way's central bulge, featuring 12 high-metallicity giants ($+1.5<[\text{Fe/H}]<+3.0$) located within 5 kpc. These stars were identified using near-infrared JWST observations. Our findings reveal bulge red giants for the first time across the entire wavelength spectrum, from 0.6 to 5 $\mu$m. The data indicate that these giants possess approximately 0.5 solar masses of non-degenerate envelope and exhibit a wide range of non-degenerate core masses (0.05--0.25 $M_{\odot}$), suggesting they originated from diverse stellar masses. Crucially, the spectra reveal significant variations in surface abundances of C, N, O, and s-process elements, with C/N ratios reaching up to 10. These variations imply that the stars have undergone third dredge-up (TDE) and possibly thermal pulse (TP) events. The study confirms that massive red giant branch (RGB) stars are not limited to low-metallicity environments and establishes spectral diagnostics capable of distinguishing between bulge and disk stellar populations based on their spectral energy distributions (SEDs) from the optical to the mid-infrared. This work lays the foundation for future investigations into the formation and evolution of the Galaxy's central massive stars. The spectra are accessible at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.10600000. This study utilizes data from programs 1038 and 1041 under the JWST First Light program.

These data are inherently complex, characterized by high dimensionality, non-linearity, and numerous missing values, which pose significant challenges for analysis. While various machine learning methods have been applied to remote sensing, there remains a lack of a comprehensive overview of approaches designed to handle high-dimensional data with missing values. This paper fills that gap by surveying and categorizing techniques for analyzing high-dimensional remote sensing data containing missing data. The survey examines how these methods address the specific nature of missing data, explores their application to both supervised and unsupervised learning tasks, and evaluates their performance. By providing this survey, we aim to inspire researchers to develop and apply innovative methods to tackle challenges in analyzing high-dimensional Earth observation data. This SHMR peaks at $z=0.2$ and subsequently declines with increasing redshift. Our analysis reveals a significant scatter in the data, which we attribute to variations in the stellar mass-to-light ratio ($\Upsilon_\star$). By correlating $\Uym_\star$ with optical color, we construct a continuous SHMR for ETGs extending to $z=2.2$. This relation indicates that at a given stellar mass, the halo mass of ETGs decreases as redshift rises from $z=0.2$ to $z=2.2$. Furthermore, we compare our results with previous studies of field and cluster ETGs, observing a redshift-dependent shift toward lower stellar masses for a given halo mass in field systems relative to cluster systems. Finally, we examine our findings in the context of galaxy formation and evolution models, specifically comparing our SHMR with predictions from the IllustrisTNG simulation. Our results align well with simulated relations for both field and cluster ETGs across redshifts of $z<2.2$. These conclusions remain robust even when accounting for potential systematic errors in the lensing-derived halo masses. Overall, our study provides strong support for the theoretical expectation that the SHMR arises from the interplay between baryonic physics and dark matter. Additionally, our methodology offers a straightforward approach to estimating the stellar mass-dependent bias of galaxy tracers in cosmological analyses. This technique is particularly valuable for determining the bias of the most luminous red galaxies at $z<2$, a parameter critical for large-scale cosmological studies. Given the anticipated increase in the number of strong lens systems with known redshifts and stellar masses from upcoming surveys, this method will prove essential for accurately modeling the bias of early-type galaxies. This study explores the feasibility of observing a specific exoplanet, LHS 2882 b, and its potential atmosphere using the photometric method. By analyzing the planet's expected thermal emission and reflected light, we determined that LHS 2882 b exhibits distinct colors compared to its parent star. We evaluated various ground-based and space-based telescopes, both with and without adaptive optics systems, to assess their capacity to detect the star-planet mass ratio of $1.1 \times 10^{-3}$. Our findings indicate that the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is capable of directly detecting LHS 2882 b at a signal-to-noise ratio of 10 within a single 1000-second observation across the 0.6–2.5 $\mu$m wavelength range. Furthermore, if LHS 2882 b possesses a hydrogen-dominated atmosphere, JWST could identify atmospheric features such as water vapor and methane within 10 hours of total observation time. Additionally, we demonstrated that the Large Synoptic Survey Telescope (LSST) can achieve a 3-sigma detection of the planet's thermal emission in as little as 1.5 nights. Consequently, the upcoming LSST and JWST offer the potential to advance exoplanet research by applying the photometric technique to systems with similar characteristics. This paper introduces a novel method for PPE (phoneme, pitch, and energy) estimation that leverages neural networks trained on discrete cosine transform (DCT) coefficients. The approach utilizes a phoneme-based Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to generate phoneme-level priors, which are then integrated with instantaneous predictions from a neural network. These priors and foreground estimates are combined using an exponential smoothing filter to derive final priors, which are merged with the smoothing filter's exponential output. Comprehensive experiments were conducted on the TIMIT database across three tasks: voiced detection, fundamental frequency (F0) estimation, and pitch tracking. The results demonstrate that this proposed approach significantly outperforms both instantaneous neural network estimates and DCT-based Gaussian Mixture Model (GMM) methods. Furthermore, the use of phoneme HMM priors consistently improves pitch tracking accuracy. Specifically, the proposed method achieves an 11.6% improvement in PPE estimation compared to instantaneous neural network approaches and a 15.8% improvement over DCT-GMM techniques. Additionally, the approach exhibits a reduced dependency on pitch magnitude; by normalizing pitch to its relative rank within a frame, the method maintains robust performance even in scenarios featuring very low pitch values. Finally, the proposed approach offers superior robustness against noise, delivering consistent results across a wide spectrum of Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) levels. The free monoid $\mathcal{A}^*$ over a finite ordered alphabet $\mathcal{A} = \{a_1, \dots, a_n\}$ comprises all words formed by concatenating letters from $\mathcal{A}$. This paper introduces and investigates a novel stochastic process known as the uniform concatenation process on $\mathcal{A}^*$, where random words are generated by successively appending random letters. For this process, we derive the exact distribution of the number of distinct letters and calculate the expected value of the number of times each specific letter appears. Additionally, we provide an efficient algorithm to determine the precise distribution for any word length. This approach complements and contrasts with methods previously used for other word generation processes, such as those found in [10] and [11], to analyze the statistics of letter occurrences.

We also examine random factorizations of $\mathcal{A}^*$, where each letter is assigned a random position upon creation. These factorizations model various processes, including random DNA evolution, random text generation, and the accumulation of knowledge. We establish a strong duality between random factorizations and random factorizations with a fixed number of factors, from which we deduce the distribution of the number of distinct letters in any given word. Using this framework, we calculate the expected number of distinct letters and the entropy of the vocabulary (the set of unique letters) for random words, random texts, and uniform factorizations. These findings are applied to model random knowledge accumulation and the random insertion of words into a dictionary. In this context, we determine the asymptotic behavior of the expected vocabulary size and entropy for texts generated by a random text writer, a politician, or a scientist.

This study examines the (3+1)-dimensional Pauli-Fierz model, where a WIMP particle interacts with fermionic matter inside the star. The WIMP possesses a non-zero mass $m_\chi$ and couples to matter via both scalar and pseudoscalar mechanisms. We analyze the stability of the star's ground state, focusing specifically on the effects of pseudoscalar interactions. Our findings indicate that star stability is contingent upon the balance between scalar and pseudoscalar contributions. These conclusions are derived from numerical solutions to the many-body Schrödinger equation, which accounts for both WIMP self-interaction and WIMP-nucleon interactions. Finally, we contrast our results with recent experimental data, discussing the implications of the derived constraints. These implications suggest that the WIMP-nucleon coupling constant is extremely small, or that the WIMP does not interact through the pseudoscalar channel. Consequently, within the framework of the Pauli-Fierz model, we determine that a WIMP with a mass $m_\chi \lesssim 100$ MeV is capable of causing stellar collapse. Additionally, our findings align with recent theoretical constraints on WIMP-nucleon coupling derived from the Pauli-Fierz model. These limits are comparable to recent experimental bounds on the pseudoscalar coupling constant $g_A$, which are constrained to be $g_A \lesssim 10^{-2}$. Within this context, we investigate the stability of both visible and hidden sectors against gravitational particle production, a phenomenon that arises dynamically in cosmological settings. Our analysis demonstrates that a simple hidden sector, consisting of a single real scalar with a simple mass term, remains stable against such production during the cosmological evolution of the visible sector across all known visible sectors, including Einstein gravity, scalar-tensor theories, Horndeski models, and a specific string-derived framework. Conversely, we identify scenarios where gravitational particle production affects the hidden sector, a mechanism that could be leveraged to constrain the viable parameter space of the visible sector. This approach offers novel avenues for testing Einstein-Ether and string-theory-based visible sectors, for which traditional collider and astrophysical limits are either extremely restrictive or entirely ineffective. Finally, we outline directions for expanding this study to other visible sectors and hidden sector configurations. Consequently, we conclude that gravitational particle production is generally negligible in typical visible-hidden sector systems. This finding is crucial for cosmological and thermodynamic analyses of dark and dark energy components, as well as for recent efforts to derive the observed radiation content of our universe from hidden sectors. These derived radiations, termed dark radiation and gravitons-inflaton (DIG) radiation, play significant roles in addressing the $H_0$ tension and other cosmological issues. Given the DIG radiation's sensitivity to gravitational particle production in the hidden sector, our work provides valuable insights for refining its predictions. Furthermore, we establish that this effect is non-existent in the DIG model derived from string theory. Our findings will be detailed in a forthcoming publication [1].

Our methodology involves examining the stability of the hidden sector by analyzing its effective potential, which is influenced by the dynamics of the visible sector. We establish that such interactions are generally absent in Einstein gravity, scalar-tensor theories, and the specific string-theory model under consideration. However, within the HDG+R and HDG+C models, the Curion scalar in the hidden sector couples to the Ricci scalar of the visible sector, driving visible sector influence on the hidden sector potential. In these cases, we assess stability by ensuring the Curion scalar field does not grow uncontrollably. We verify this by confirming that its kinetic energy remains non-negative and that its equation of state allows for stable evolution. Our results indicate that gravitational particle production is typically insignificant for the DIG signal. This conclusion holds significant implications for recent attempts to resolve the $H_0$ tension using DIG radiation

We demonstrate a color-plus-monocular camera setup for depth estimation, enabling two key applications: (1) improved in-vehicle and obstacle detection for autonomous driving, and (2) enhanced autonomous flight for drones. Our proposed autoencoder-based system achieves this by utilizing color data from the Raspberry Pi 3 and depth data from the Raspberry Pi Zero W to generate a fused depth map. This approach is specifically beneficial for dual-camera configurations and eliminates any latency, as it functions in an in-parallel manner. Our evaluations across multiple scenarios show that this method significantly outperforms current single RBD-based and object detection algorithms in low-texture conditions and during motion. Specifically, it addresses the number of parts divisible by k in partitions of n where every part's multiplicity is strictly less than k, represented by ak(n). The study offers a combinatorial proof by adapting Glaisher's classic bijection and derives a generating function, which is subsequently analyzed to establish combinatorial identities for a(k,n). The paper concludes with a combinatorial interpretation of ak(n) as the sum of binomial coefficients \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} ak-1(i). This interface, separating a Josephson coupling anisotropy component ($J$) from a charge isotropy component ($c$), is critical for achieving high-temperature superconductivity. Our findings indicate that the kinetic transport across this interface is constrained by the low group velocity of the critical current carriers. Consequently, to enhance transport, we suggest using a c-axis cut of the $d$-wave critical current gap as the optimal crystal orientation. Furthermore, we estimate that the $c$-axis critical current density could rise to approximately $10^{11}$ A/cm$^2$. These insights provide a theoretical foundation for developing high-capacity Josephson junctions with critical current densities comparable to those in the ab-plane. Such advancements are essential for constructing high-resolution quantum circuits, including qubits, necessary for future quantum computers. Additionally, these results support the design of high-field, high-resolution SQUID magnetometers capable of detecting minute magnetic fields, such as the nanotesla levels associated with brain activity, thereby aiding the development of advanced magnetoencephalography systems. Finally, the proposed high-$J_c$ anisotropic junctions offer a viable pathway for creating high-energy qubits, which are vital components for next-generation quantum computers. To achieve this, we recommend employing high-quality c-axis cut crystals, such as La$_2$CuO$_4$-based materials, which currently exhibit the highest high-field $c$-axis critical current densities. Theoretical and experimental investigations into the origin of the high anisotropy in these cuprates are also necessary to guide the development of even higher-energy qubits. In intrinsic systems, however, the formation of such moments requires explicit symmetry breaking in the Hamiltonian. We demonstrate that in the InAs/InP superlattice system, local magnetic moments generated in InP layers originate from the penetration (spill-out) of InAs valence band wave functions. This phenomenon occurs due to the unusually large lattice mismatch between the two materials and is amplified by the extremely thin interface barriers. The induced magnetization in InAs bilayers has previously been documented, a finding supported by both experimental data and various theoretical models. Our results provide additional evidence for this effect, highlighting a significant overlap of wave functions across the interface that creates magnetic moments in the P-based alloy through a spontaneous "magnetic" bilayer effect. This mechanism offers a general approach to engineering local magnetic moments at heterointerfaces within semiconductor systems. Furthermore, the same theoretical framework can explain experimental observations of spin polarization within the bulk of InP layers. Finally, we propose that this interface effect holds broad potential for designing magnetic phenomena at semiconductor interfaces. To validate this, we present additional experimental data from x-ray magnetic circular dichroism (XMCD) studies on (InAs$_{x}$P$_{1-x}$/InP) bilayers, which corroborate the theoretical predictions. These new experimental findings confirm the magnetic character of the InAs bilayer and quantify the magnetic moment induced in the InP bilayer. Specifically, for a 10 Å InAs bilayer, we observe the generation of approximately 0.025 $\mu_{B}$/a.u. of local magnetic moment in the InP bilayer. These results demonstrate that even a monolayer of InAs can trigger the formation of local magnetic moments in InP. This phenomenon is particularly relevant for ultra-thin InAs bilayers grown on InP substrates, a configuration frequently employed in existing experimental studies of interface magnetism in InAs-based semiconductor systems. Our findings indicate that the magnetic moment induced in InP bilayers by InAs bilayers aligns with experimental data regarding the total magnetic moment in InAs$_{x}$P$_{1-x}$InP ternary alloys, a result that has previously been difficult to explain. We attribute the total magnetic moment in these alloys to the superposition of two components: the moment present in intrinsic InP and the moment induced in InP by InAs. Specifically, we introduce a generalized ansatz that enables the reduction of the dimensionally reduced Euler-Lagrange equations to a four-dimensional system of first-order ordinary differential equations. These dimensionally reduced models are particularly valuable for analyzing the stability of kink solitons. Our approach highlights a broad class of two-field, one-component kink solutions, with a primary focus on meta-stable solitons within the Standard Model of particle physics. Notably, we examine models featuring a doublet scalar field and a complex singlet scalar, which is relevant for generating a small neutrino mass via the see-saw mechanism and potentially driving electroweak baryon number violation. Furthermore, we explore scenarios where the doublet scalar possesses a complex vacuum expectation value, a condition that may enable dark matter production through the "freeze-in" process. These findings are particularly pertinent to recent investigations into the cosmological production of dark matter via scalar field interactions. Additionally, our analysis of soliton configurations in interacting scalar theories offers utility for various other areas of theoretical and mathematical physics. This work is particularly significant for researchers exploring the vacuum structure of the standard model to determine if our universe corresponds to a false vacuum state. Finally, one of our derived dimensionally reduced models, $\phi^4$-Yang-Mills, is of interest to mathematicians studying soliton configurations in non-abelian gauge theories. Finally, we anticipate that our findings will be particularly relevant to recent investigations into the cosmological production of dark matter via scalar field interactions.

While the term historically referred to items printed on low-quality paper using basic, often daisy-chained, offset printing methods, it currently encompasses various types of unpublished manuscripts, including drafts intended for future journal submission, conference papers, or inclusion in edited volumes. Preprints may also be submitted to specialized preprint archives for community feedback before formal submission. Although some view preprints as informal or preliminary due to their lack of formal peer review, others utilize them to disseminate research rapidly, share findings with the community, and establish priority. This chapter examines the etymology and evolution of the term "preprint," explores its diverse contemporary uses, and addresses the associated challenges and opportunities. It further addresses critical questions regarding the definition, classification, and characterization of preprints, as well as the development of metrics to evaluate their impact. Finally, the text highlights current initiatives and future directions in preprint research, with a specific focus on the emerging role of preprints in scientific information retrieval.

This work introduces a novel method for detecting and classifying speech acts within dialogue. The detection phase employs a BERT-based neural network trained on a newly compiled dataset of first-person statements from 20 different languages, achieving 90% accuracy. For classification, these statements are organized into five categories: commitments, commitments of quality, assertions, explanations, and explanations of attitude. A coarse-grained classification scheme was created to enhance comparability across languages, though a fine-grained category system is also provided. The classification algorithm, which utilizes BERT, operates effectively in a low-resource setting using only 10 examples per speech act per language for training, yielding an F1 score of 61%. The study's results demonstrate that dialogue acts are present and consistent across all examined languages, and that BERT-based classifiers can successfully identify and categorize them even with limited in-domain examples.

Among these, body-centered cubic HEAs stand out for their exceptional mechanical properties, including high strength and ductility. However, the atomic disorder within HEAs creates substantial challenges for structural characterization. While total scattering combined with reverse Monte Carlo (RMC) refinement offers a viable solution, it demands extensive laboratory time on neutron or synchrotron sources. This study demonstrates that a straightforward, low-cost neutron total scattering experiment can yield crucial data for modeling HEA structures. We utilized a 50-minute scan on a 1-inch wide sample to collect scattering data from five HEAs, covering the range from 1 to 50 Å⁻¹. These datasets were subsequently employed to construct models of the HEAs using RMC methods. The resulting models accurately reflect the experimental pair distribution functions, confirming that a 50-minute collection period is adequate for well-ordered HEAs. This approach enables the maximum utilization of beam time at research facilities like the Oak Ridge National Laboratory's Spallation Neutron Source. Furthermore, the methodology is extensible to other techniques, such as ab initio total scattering and diffraction analysis. This workflow establishes a foundation for investigating various local atomic environments within complex materials. This study employs the well-posed stochastic SIR model, which incorporates infection and demographic stochasticity, to investigate the dynamics of COVID-19 within the United States. Our analysis reveals that the trajectory of infectious cases is inherently stochastic, driven by large random fluctuations that cannot be captured by traditional deterministic approaches. Consequently, predicting the future course of the pandemic in the US becomes an impossible task. Furthermore, we introduce a novel coarse-grained stochastic model capable of efficiently simulating the pandemic's macroscopic behavior. This model utilizes time-resolved data to estimate the effective reproduction number ($R_{eff}$) and the pandemic's trajectory, offering a robust framework for monitoring infectious disease outbreaks. We successfully applied this model to track COVID-19 data from the US and other nations, demonstrating its ability to identify the pandemic's turning points. These findings underscore the critical role of non-pharmaceutical interventions in altering infectious disease dynamics. Ultimately, this research provides a theoretical foundation for future studies aiming to model infectious disease spread using time-series data. Additionally, the proposed model is versatile and can be extended to predict the trajectories of other phenomena, including viral and bacterial infections, wildfires, and financial market fluctuations. Finally, we have made this model publicly accessible via an online application. The associated code and documentation are available at https://uscodetrack.github.io/USCOVID/. In this work, we introduce a quantum protocol enabling a client with no quantum capabilities to efficiently validate a classical function computed by a quantum server. Previously, Vazirani and Vidale proposed a method for pointwise verification, where a client checks the correctness of a single function output. Our approach ensures information-theoretic privacy for the function, meaning the function is never revealed to the verifier. Furthermore, our protocol demonstrates that amortized verification is more efficient than repeatedly performing pointwise checks. Specifically, the classical communication complexity per input is reduced from $O(n)$ bits in the pointwise case to $O(\log n)$ bits. Additionally, the protocol achieves nearly optimal efficiency, with a complexity of $O(n\log n)$ qubits of classical communication, compared to the $O(n)$ classical bits required for pointwise verification. The core of our method relies on a new private information retrieval (PIR) scheme, where a client with no quantum knowledge retrieves a single item from a quantum database containing $N$ items, using a message of length $O(n)$. This construction is almost as efficient as PIR for classical inputs, which typically requires a message length of $O(n\log N)$. The foundation of our PIR construction is a novel quantum code, the quantum Hadamard code, which is also applicable to other areas. For instance, it can be utilized to create a quantum version of the classical point-functional model, where a client with no quantum knowledge verifies a computation by interacting with $O(\log N)$ servers, each holding an $O(n)$-qubit register. This is asymptotically more efficient than pointwise verification, which usually requires $O(n)$ servers. In both pointwise and point-functional scenarios, our method offers significant improvements in input length, server round complexity, and communication cost per round. Finally, we establish a lower bound on the quantum communication complexity for pointwise verification, proving that any protocol achieving amortized verification must use at least $\Omega(n/\log n)$ qubits of classical communication. This result confirms that our protocol provides nearly optimal efficiency.

This study introduces DeepSpectrogramNet, a novel end-to-end deep learning framework designed for automated diabetic retinopathy (DR) classification. Question Answering (QA) stands as a pivotal area within natural language processing, demanding robust models capable of identifying relevant information within unstructured text to provide precise responses. Although pre-trained language models have significantly advanced the field, they often underperform when handling long documents or those with complex structures. To overcome these limitations, we introduce Longformer-BiDA, a novel approach that integrates the Longformer architecture with bidirectional attention mechanisms for document-level QA. Our method retains the efficiency of bidirectional attention for short contexts while effectively managing long documents and intricate structures through the introduction of token types. Extensive experiments conducted on two benchmark datasets, SQuAD and DuReader, confirm the effectiveness of our proposed framework. The results highlight the model's superior performance in accurately localizing key information within long and complex documents. Code and data are available at https://github.com/ashwinbhat/Longformer-BiDA.

Controlling quantum systems via measurements and classical or quantum loops is a rapidly evolving area of research. This study examines the stellar content of MSFRs in the nearby (d ~ 1.4 Mpc) Centaurus A galaxy by analyzing HST/WFC3/UVIS and NICMOS images alongside archival data. We identify 107 sources across 11 MSFRs, with 89 classified as single stars and 18 as clusters. By fitting synthetic colors to these classifications, we determine stellar masses and stellar population ages. Our results indicate that the majority of the galaxy's star formation is concentrated in a few dominant complexes, which collectively contain approximately 90% of the total stellar mass. These dominant complexes are primarily single star sources, defined as individual stars or small groups (<10) lacking extended structures. The stellar mass-to-light ratio for these dominant sources is 1000 +/- 100 M_sun/L_sun, suggesting a predominantly young population. The median age of the single sources is 10 Myr, with a 90% confidence interval ranging from 1 to 100 Myr. Furthermore, the stellar mass and age distributions of the dominant complexes show a strong correlation, with a best-fit slope of 0.5 +/- 0.1. Finally, we observe that the stellar mass and age distributions of the single sources differ significantly between the MSFRs, implying that the star formation process varies from one complex to another within the same galaxy. The age distribution of the dominant sources correlates with the HII region size, with larger regions being younger. This aligns with the idea that MSFRs evolve through the sequential growth of dominant complexes, which are young, followed by the development of smaller sources. The older, smaller sources may result from the fragmentation of the dominant complex or the accretion of external gas. The MSFRs in Centaurus A appear to be in the early stages of this evolutionary sequence. The HII regions in Centaurus A are not dominated by a single massive complex, unlike those in the Milky Way or M82. This suggests that the evolution of MSFRs is not uniform across different galaxies. The lack of a dominant complex in Centaurus A may be due to the galaxy's low stellar mass, which is insufficient to trigger the gravitational instability thought to drive the formation of a dominant complex in more massive galaxies. This study investigates the stripe phase within the two-dimensional Hubbard model by employing a novel series expansion technique called Nth-order self-energy perturbation (NSEP). We examine stripes in square and honeycomb lattices across various orders, observing that the results for the stripe phase are nearly identical in both lattice types. Specifically, we document the suppression of antiferromagnetic ordering, the development of bond incommensurability, and the impact of bandwidth on stripe stability. Furthermore, by analyzing spin and charge densities along with their correlations, we determine the nature of stripe instabilities. Our findings indicate that low-order approximations are insufficient for capturing these effects; however, by utilizing cancellation between self-energy terms, we successfully identify the characteristics of stripes. Ultimately, we conclude that the stripe phase remains robust even at the metallic band limit. These results offer valuable insights into stripe instabilities in cuprate superconductors. Additionally, by comparing our findings with those of the dynamical mean-field theory, we observe discrepancies regarding phase separation and the phase diagram of stripes. These inconsistencies highlight the necessity of developing more advanced computational methods to gain a deeper understanding of stripe instabilities in correlated systems. In this work, we present our novel NSEP method, which has not previously been applied to investigate stripe instabilities in two-dimensional flat-band systems. Finally, we note that the methodology used here can be extended to explore other many-body effects, such as charge density waves and nematicity. Reed-Muller codes, a family of error-correcting codes, are extensively researched due to their utility in various applications. Answer: Gröbner bases are a fundamental instrument in elimination theory, a field dedicated to deriving properties of projected sets from those of the original ones. For instance, they enable the elimination of variables from a system of polynomial equations, allowing one to determine if a system has solutions independent of specific variables. Furthermore, they play a crucial role in algebraic geometry by characterizing the properties of algebraic sets through their defining ideals.

Question: Can you provide an example demonstrating the utility of Gröbner bases in elimination theory?

Answer: Consider the polynomial ring $R = k[x_1, \ldots, x_n]$ and an ideal $I \subset R$ generated by a set of polynomials $G = \{g_1, \ldots, g_m\}$. Suppose we aim to eliminate the variables $x_{n-k+1}, \ldots, x_n$. We can achieve this by selecting an elimination order on the monomials of $R$ such that all monomials involving these variables are leading terms of $G$. The set $G'$ obtained by removing these leading terms then generates the elimination ideal $I \cap (k[x_1, \ldots, x_{n-k}])$. This process can be iterated to eliminate additional variables.

In the realm of web service composition, two primary strategies exist: imperative composition, which manages explicit control flow, and declarative composition, which relies on constraints to define desired outcomes. We introduce a unified framework that incorporates elements of both, presenting a new class of web service compositions known as Array-based Web Service Processes (arWOPs). These arWOPs feature deterministic control flow governed by data conditions, alongside both declarative and imperative invocations of web services that manipulate data. We define arWOPs formally as a subset of data-aware imperative web service processes characterized by specific properties. A key distinction of our framework is the introduction of reasoning capabilities for arWOPs, enabling the automatic synthesis of these processes from high-level constraints. We provide a formal syntax and semantics for arWOPs, along with a directional synthesis algorithm that generates them from a new class of goals. This approach ensures that the resulting arWOPs adhere to the specifications, are free from redundancy, and minimize service invocations. This article examines Private Location Routing, a specific application where a user (client) submits a sequence of destination points to a server for pathfinding, all while keeping the destinations confidential. We present a fully homomorphic encryption-based scheme that allows a server to compute shortest paths on a road network without learning the client's locations. The scheme maintains efficiency regarding both computational and memory requirements on the client and server sides. Privacy is ensured against a potentially malicious server that can perform only polynomial-time operations. We validate the scheme's performance using real-world road networks from the US, UK, and EU. The results demonstrate that the scheme achieves a substantial privacy guarantee with reasonable efficiency. Furthermore, the approach is general enough to incorporate additional features, such as guiding a client through multiple locations in sequence. To our knowledge, this is the first proposal capable of achieving such privacy guarantees. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/abhishekgupta10/PLR.

In concurrent work, [FGK+21] also addresses Private Location Routing but assumes the server is trusted, whereas our approach functions in a trusted-server model. Their method relies on the client generating all cryptographic keys and performing the most computationally intensive encryption and decryption steps, resulting in higher client-side overhead. In contrast, our scheme requires minimal client-side computation. Additionally, they do not protect against a malicious server, while our scheme does. Finally, they offer no efficiency guarantees regarding memory usage.

### 1. Introduction

#### 1.1. Background and Motivation

The proliferation of location-dependent services has made it increasingly difficult for users to maintain their privacy. For example, if a user frequently visits the same locations, an observer could infer details about the user's identity, habits, and other sensitive information. Consequently, there is a growing demand for systems that deliver location services while preserving privacy. This paper addresses a scenario where a client requests a route to a server, which then transmits the route back to the client in an encrypted format for decryption. The server must determine the path without accessing the client's locations, and the client must not perform any computations other than encrypting its request and decrypting the response. This setup models a trusted execution environment for the server, where code and data are protected from external attacks.

While this phenomenon has been extensively studied in the context of globally coupled identical oscillators, this paper extends its analysis to networks comprising different types of oscillators with arbitrary connectivity. We derive precise synchronization conditions and demonstrate the construction of numerically computable potential functions that delineate the basins of attraction for various synchronization states. The utility of these findings is highlighted through their application to a system of two globally coupled clusters, each containing two units. Furthermore, we propose a method for designing group synchronization in arbitrary systems by strategically modifying the coupling structure of isolated units. The feasibility of this approach is validated using a network of three globally coupled chaotic Rössler oscillators. Our results offer valuable insights for efficiently constructing multimorph neural networks and robustly encoding information within them. Additionally, multimorph neural networks possess strong potential for multi-pattern associative memory, a critical requirement for cognitive functions such as pattern recognition. Finally, we emphasize that group synchronization is fundamental to numerous physical systems, including fermionic and bosonic quantum systems, and can serve as a metric for disorder within a system. As an example, we utilize group synchronization to distinguish between different quantum phases in systems of interacting bosons. These insights are presented through the lens of an effective Ising model, which proves instrumental in analyzing group states and phase transitions in systems of coupled oscillators. This study establishes a direct link between the physics of synchronization and statistical mechanics. The approach is applicable to a broad spectrum of physical, biological, and engineering systems that exhibit various synchronization phenomena. large language models (LLMs). Our findings indicate that LMs exhibit significant bias toward the "wikicity" of their training data, displaying a strong preference for Wikipedia over other non-Wikipedia sources. We introduce the first metric to quantify this preferential treatment, named "Wikipedia Preference" (WIP), and demonstrate its strong correlation with higher wikicity. WIP reveals that non-Wikipedia domains are underrepresented in model outputs, whereas domains present in the training data show a preference ratio exceeding 2:1. Additionally, we observe that WIP remains robust across various evaluation methods and is positively influenced by model size and contextual richness. To address this issue, we tested several mitigation strategies, including in-context learning with diverse training data, prompt-based self-reflection, and output-based re-ranking. Among these, re-ranking based on a non-Wikipedia source classifier achieved the greatest reduction in WIP, with only a minor impact on non-Wikipedia source performance. This approach outperforms other mitigation methods by significantly lowering WIP while maintaining a high preference ratio for non-Wikipedia domains. We make our source-level training and evaluation datasets, along with the associated models, accessible at https://github.com/lyy-0314/llm-wikicity-bias.

Our analysis highlights that well-known exact solutions for the Einstein equations—specifically those that do not depend on the cosmological constant—also satisfy the field equations derived from the Cotton tensor. Furthermore, we derive a new class of exact solutions for asymptotically flat spacetimes, characterized by an anisotropic fluid source and a potential function, which represent exact solutions to the Cotton field equations. Additionally, we identify and discuss other known non-Einstein exact solutions of the form $ds^2=-f(r)dt^2+g(r)^{-1}dr^2+r^2(d\theta^2+\sin^2\theta d\phi^2)$ that represent valid solutions to the Cotton field equations. Finally, we present a method for generating novel exact solutions within the framework of the Cotton tensor. These findings suggest that the Cotton tensor offers valuable insights into gravitation, potentially yielding new exact solutions that differ significantly from those obtained via the standard Einstein formulation. The Cotton tensor offers precise results for large distances and provides a means to explore nontrivial new exact solutions in the near field. In the near field, the Cotton formulation reveals new aspects of black holes and other compact objects, such as white holes and gravastars. Furthermore, the Cotton tensor appears capable of describing the universe's evolution without a cosmological constant, a capability that the Einstein formulation lacks. Consequently, the Cotton tensor presents an alternative approach to understanding the universe's history, potentially offering new perspectives on why the current accelerating expansion of the universe remains unexplained within the general theory of relativity. The distribution examines configurational entropy, such as that found in polymer systems, relative to an energy component defined by the user's specified potential. The method demonstrates the practical application of a recently published algorithm [1], which addresses a significant hurdle in Boltzmann sampling: the inefficiency of the conventional Metropolis-Hastings (MH) method when the Boltzmann distribution's derivative is complex or costly to compute. The new approach, which we refer to as the "method of continuous annealing," iteratively transforms a simple reference probability distribution into the target distribution. During each iteration, variables couple more strongly to one another and to the potential, causing the system to gradually shift from a high-probability reference state to the target Boltzmann distribution. At every step, the algorithm employs the MH method to generate samples from this evolving distribution. We show that this algorithm successfully produces samples from the target distribution, provided the initial reference distribution is sufficiently simple and the potential and coupling strengths are not excessively large. Furthermore, we illustrate how the method allows users to bypass difficulties in analytically or approximately defining a reference distribution, as the algorithm automatically determines an optimal reference distribution that samples the system near a user-defined energy target. This capability is particularly beneficial for systems lacking an obvious reference state, offering an entirely annealing-based solution. Introduced by Rudzicz and Ng (2010), the hdr lasso demonstrates superior performance in high-dimensional scenarios compared to traditional lasso methods for ranking. However, its primary limitation lies in the absence of an efficient solution algorithm, necessitating the use of suboptimal approaches that significantly increase computational costs and compromise result quality. In global optimization, this dilemma specifically concerns if a globally optimal parameter set can be identified from noisy data. We demonstrate that for a specific class of inverse problems—linear combination of a fixed dictionary with $\ell_1$-regularization—the solution becomes identifiable under certain conditions related to noise levels, dictionary size, and signal-to-noise ratios. Specifically, we establish that a small number of highly noisy data points can prevent identifiability. Furthermore, within the identifiable regime, we propose a randomized algorithm with guaranteed outcomes to determine if a given solution is globally optimal. Numerical experiments on both synthetic and real datasets illustrate the trade-offs among noise, dictionary complexity, and the frequency of identifiability. These experiments also show that simple heuristic approaches can significantly speed up the process while maintaining quality, although their performance varies depending on the specific problem context. Finally, we provide an open-source implementation of our algorithm, accessible at https://github.com/robertfischer/IsMySolutionOptimal.

Keywords: inverse problems, global optimization, $\ell_1$-regularization, identifiability, randomized algorithm, guaranteed outcomes, synthetic data, real data, computational complexity, open-source implementation.

While these models offer significant benefits, they also introduce risks, including the potential for malicious actors to manipulate them. This paper offers a comprehensive overview of adversarial attacks and defenses within machine learning, detailing how adversaries can exploit these models and the strategies employed to mitigate such threats. Deep learning models have achieved remarkable success across numerous domains, yet their "black-box" nature hinders trust in their decision-making processes. Although recent efforts have attempted to explain these models, a unified framework for their evaluation remains absent. To address this gap, we introduce XLE, a comprehensive evaluation framework designed to assess the explainability of machine learning models. XLE incorporates a diverse set of criteria and employs automated methods to measure how well explainability techniques satisfy these standards. The framework is intended to be inclusive, allowing for the easy integration of new methods and evaluation criteria. We have conducted a large-scale study using a wide range of existing explainability approaches, revealing that most current solutions perform poorly according to XLE's assessments. Our contributions include: (1) a systematic review of existing literature on model explainability, (2) the proposal of a holistic evaluation framework with 19 criteria, (3) the development of novel automated evaluation methods, and (4) an extensive empirical study featuring 810,000 experiments across 100,000 test cases. XLE is openly available at  and has been recognized as a Finalist for the 2022 ACM-IMS Karp Manuscript Award.

This work has been acknowledged as a Finalist for the 2022 ACM-IMS Karap Manuscript Award.

Self-supervised learning has emerged as a dominant approach for pre-training models on massive unlabeled datasets, subsequently fine-tuning them with smaller labeled ones. While this strategy has proven highly effective in computer vision and natural language processing, its application to structured data has been limited. We introduce S4, a self-supervised pre-training algorithm tailored for structured data, and evaluate it on tabular datasets. Our results demonstrate that S4 can pre-train on datasets roughly 100 times larger than those used for fine-tuning, achieving performance on par with models fine-tuned exclusively on the small dataset. We also explore various pre-training objectives and adapter techniques for fine-tuning, offering insights into their relative strengths. The code is available at https://github.com/OPAL-Tabular/S4.

Text-to-SQL translation has become a focal point of recent research, yet existing methods often fail to generalize well to new datasets. To address this, we propose a novel self-supervised pre-training strategy for SQL generation. Our method leverages unannotated SQL schemas and their corresponding tabular data to create a new pre-training objective. This approach not only mitigates the need for large sets of annotated SQL queries but also significantly enhances model performance on new datasets. Empirical evaluations confirm that our method yields state-of-the-art results on two benchmark SQL translation tasks. Code and data can be found at https://github.com/ai4db/text2sql.

The micro-component, representing internal deformation, is captured through a finite-dimensional space of compact support trajectories. Error estimates are derived in a posteriori form using residuals relative to specific norms. The micro-component satisfies an ordinary differential equation (ODE) that is coupled with the partial differential equation (PDE) governing fluid motion. By leveraging standard elliptic estimates, the framework establishes error bounds consisting of PDE components (fluid flow), ODE components (internal dynamics), and a coupling term. Since the model relies on the Euler-Lagrange equation of a non-linear functional, standard FEM convergence theory does not directly apply. Instead, we derive convergence results by applying appropriate compactness theorems to the sequence of solutions obtained via the Galerkin method. Finally, numerical experiments utilizing specific finite-dimensional trajectory spaces demonstrate the effectiveness of the error estimates. These simulations compare solutions against those from a high-resolution fine-mesh simulation and validate the accuracy of the proposed error bounds.

Significant research has focused on efficient parameterized algorithms, particularly those achieving parameterized sublinear running times, while maintaining a kernel of size $O(f(\sigma) \cdot \sigma^{O(1)})$, where $\sigma$ denotes the target parameter and $f$ is a function of another parameter $g$. This study examines scenarios where a kernel size of $2^{O(g)} \cdot \sigma^{O(1)}$ is attainable. We introduce the concept of parameterized sublinear time for $\sigma$ given $g$, and demonstrate its feasibility across various models, including deterministic, randomized, and a novel Monte Carlo framework. Additionally, we present a novel lower bound technique applicable to parameterized sublinear-time kernels, yielding negative results even under the relaxed Monte Carlo definition. Our initial application of this approach is to the Feedback Vertex Set problem, offering the first algorithm with a kernel of size $2^{O(g)}$ (under the stronger deterministic model) and a corresponding result for Densest $k$-Subgraph. Furthermore, we develop a general method to construct parameterized Monte Carlo time algorithms with an error probability no greater than $2^{-\Omega(n/g)}$ from deterministic ones running in $2^{O(g)}$ time, a tool we apply to obtain a parameterized Monte Carlo algorithm with a $k^{O(g)}$ kernel and a parameterized deterministic algorithm with a $k^{O(g)\log k}$ kernel, both targeting Feedback Vertex Set. Finally, we establish a limitation on parameterized Monte Carlo kernels by proving a lower bound of $k^{\Omega(g)}$ for Densest $k$-Subgraph, assuming the Densest $k$-Subgraph Conjecture. This lower bound relies on a general technique applicable to any parameterized problem, contingent on the existence of a family of hard instances with a specific structure. Combined with a parameterized Monte Carlo algorithm, this method yields a lower bound of $k^{\Omega(g)}$ for any parameterized problem admitting such an algorithm. Notably, this result is the sole parameterized lower bound known to be superlinear in $k$. Our findings are the initial step toward a complete classification of parameterized sublinear-time algorithms, specifically by addressing the threshold between $2^{O(g)}$ and $k^{O(g)}$. This classification is ultimately achieved by our earlier work on the Densest $k$-Subgraph problem

We introduce a mathematical framework where an initial network of opinionated agents undergoes two concurrent processes: one agent randomly replaces another, and the probability edges form or dissolve based on the similarity of their neighbors' opinions. Through analytical methods, we determine the precise conditions under which the system stabilizes at a single dominant opinion versus a state where multiple stable coexistences of opinions are possible. Our model offers a fresh perspective on opinion dynamics, differing from traditional approaches by allowing the network structure to emerge endogenously. These mechanisms could explain why certain environments foster unified viewpoints while others lead to fragmented, polarized outcomes. Furthermore, our approach sheds light on various phenomena in evolutionary games played on dynamic networks, including the spread of cooperation, the adoption of innovations, rumor propagation, and the evolution of norms. Numerical simulations confirm the accuracy of our theoretical predictions. Ultimately, this work opens a new avenue for investigating opinion dynamics within networks that evolve internally.

**I. Introduction**

The interior geometry of charged black holes presents intriguing possibilities. In an asymptotically anti-de Sitter (AdS) context, the black hole interior is well understood through the AdS/CFT correspondence, where it corresponds to a specific phase of the boundary field theory. Specifically, above a critical temperature, the interior of an uncharged black hole is trivial, containing only a thermal bath. However, when a global U(1) charge is introduced, a charged scalar field undergoes condensation, transforming the interior into a region filled with the condensate. This phenomenon mirrors the boundary theory developing a condensate for a spontaneously symmetry-broken phase. Consequently, the black hole interior can be viewed as a dual representation of the boundary theory's condensate.

In asymptotically flat spacetimes, however, such interpretations are absent because there is no dual field theory. This paper investigates whether the concept of an interior condensate can still be meaningfully defined. We demonstrate that this is indeed possible within a newly discovered family of charged black holes. These solutions possess hairy horizons and feature a region outside the event horizon where the scalar field is non-trivial. As the charge increases from zero while keeping the mass constant, the scalar field develops a non-trivial profile, creating a finite region outside the horizon where the field is active. This region corresponds to the "black hole skin" explored in previous studies.

The most compelling aspect of these solutions lies within the event horizon. As an observer traverses the horizon and moves toward the singularity, they encounter regions where both the scalar field and its gradient are non-negligible. This indicates that an observer would directly experience the black hole's "interior condensate." This scenario is analogous to the phase diagram of a charged black hole in AdS, where the interior structure is dual to the boundary theory. 64Ni nucleus has been a subject of extensive study and debate due to its significant impact on nuclear structure and astrophysical processes. This study presents a comprehensive experimental investigation of 64Ni's ground-state structure by populating its first two 3- states via a 58Fe + 58Ni fusion reaction. A newly developed, high-efficiency double-sided silicon strip detector (DSSSD) was utilized to identify the reaction products. Excitation energies, relative energies, and absolute B(E M1) values for these doubly excited states are reported, marking the first-ever experimental observation of a non-zero value for the |E( M1) - E(E1)| relative energy. These findings align with existing experimental data and support the configuration-mixing scenario predicted by state-of-the-art theoretical models. The newly measured B(E M1) values provide crucial constraints for refining nuclear structure models, which are essential for accurately predicting key nuclear properties required in astrophysical environments. Consequently, these results have important implications for nucleosynthesis models. Furthermore, the high-efficiency detection technique employed here offers a promising pathway for exploring nuclear structure in isotopes that are scarce or inaccessible using conventional methods. The DSSSD technology is particularly well-suited for this purpose, as it enables the detection of 66Nu nuclei produced through charged-particle evaporation channels in wide-beam experiments. This capability is critical for investigating even-N, even-Z nuclei with masses ranging from 50 to 100, thereby significantly advancing our understanding of nuclear astrophysics. The paper concludes with a discussion of the techniques employed and their potential applications. Keywords: Nuclear Fusion, Nuclear Structure, Nuclear Astrophysics.

To leverage these extensive visual and sparse auditory resources for capturing rich physical properties, we introduce the novel Sparseround() method, which facilitates bidirectional mapping between sparse acoustic inputs and dense visual representations. Specifically, Sparseround() enhances the acoustic encoder by iteratively refining acoustic embeddings through visual feedback rounds. Consequently, the acoustic encoder gains the capability to grasp dense physical attributes of objects despite being trained solely on sparse examples. Our approach requires no visual data during training and successfully generalizes to unseen objects using as little as a single acoustic example. Empirical results demonstrate that our method significantly surpasses current state-of-the-art techniques in both unsupervised zero-shot and few-shot scenarios. Object detection and segmentation applications utilizing our acoustic embeddings also markedly outperform existing solutions. Furthermore, benchmarking across multiple tasks reveals that our acoustic embeddings capture richer physical attributes than existing sparse acoustic methods. We have made all necessary code and data publicly available to reproduce our results and compare them against other approaches. In this work, we present an efficient and effective approach for learning acoustic embeddings of everyday objects from sparse data by mapping acoustic inputs to visual representations. These rich visual representations of physical properties substantially enhance various downstream tasks, including object recognition, detection, and segmentation. Our evaluations on multiple benchmarks indicate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art solutions. Key contributions include: (1) demonstrating that visual representations derived from repeatedly mapping around sparse acoustic data using abundant visual information substantially improve object acoustic embeddings; (2) proving that our method achieves superior performance compared to existing approaches in multiple-task acoustic embedding benchmarks using only sparse acoustic data; (3) revealing that our acoustic embeddings capture richer physical properties than existing methods; and (4) confirming that these embeddings substantially outperform existing solutions in object detection and segmentation tasks. All code and data are publicly available at: https://github.com/leeyoonseok/SparseRound.

Model particles within this system are dual: they are magnetic, enabling control via external fields, and sticky, as they can adhere to one another. We present a theoretical framework that predicts a three-stage viscosity response to increasing external field strength. The first stage involves the alignment of spherical particles into chains along the field direction. The second stage sees these chains bundling together to form network structures. The final stage occurs when magnetic interactions overcome the cost of confining flux within the particles, causing them to magnetize and the networks to percolate globally. Our predictions align with existing literature and experimental data. Furthermore, we propose a novel experimental setup to test these phenomena, designed to measure the rheological properties of ferrogel networks while varying the degree of particle magnetization. This work lays the groundwork for developing materials with tunable rheology and network structures, which could have significant applications in soft robotics and the biomedical field. Additionally, our model suggests that similar multi-scale behaviors could emerge in other systems containing networks that transition between different states. Finally, this research opens new avenues for studying the fundamental physics of sticky charged particles in strong magnetic fields. Specifically, it paves the way for experiments examining how network structure evolves as particles transition from a charged state to a neutral, magnetizable state. Such experiments could yield insights into the sticky particle limit of the Vlasov-Maxwell-Boltzmann equations. These networks, which possess both gel and fluid characteristics, are also expected to display complex failure modes, including the formation of cracks and remnant structures oriented perpendicular to the field. Understanding these mechanisms is crucial for leveraging these materials in soft robotics and biomedical applications. Furthermore, these systems could facilitate the study of charged particle dynamics in complex, remnant network structures. This capability would enable more sophisticated investigations into collective phenomena, such as diffusion and hydrodynamics, within networks of charged particles. Such research could advance our understanding of electrostatic and electrohydrodynamic effects in various contexts, from biological systems to colloidal assemblies. These materials could also serve as models for studying the self-assembly of nanoscale objects into functional structures. Through a lab experiment involving 128 engineers, we found that PSI significantly increases search efficiency, saving approximately 30% of the time spent interacting with search results. Furthermore, users are nearly three times more likely to click on non-advertisement results when PSI is active. These advantages stem from enhanced query comprehension and the utilization of the user's search history. Our findings demonstrate that for engineers—whose online tasks are inherently complex and information-intensive—personalized search substantially improves efficiency by leveraging historical data. Consequently, we encourage other researchers to assess the benefits and drawbacks of PSI within their own domains.

Although numerous studies have explored how to improve the relevance of personalized search results (PSI) for individual users, there is a scarcity of research on the mechanisms driving users to click on these results and how those mechanisms can be optimized. This paper introduces a novel framework to analyze click behavior on PSI. Based on this model, we conducted a lab experiment to identify factors influencing click decisions. The findings reveal that click behavior is driven by two primary factors: the perceived personalization quality of the content and the user's confidence in the query. We developed two techniques to optimize these drivers: (1) employing neural machine translation to generate more personalized results, and (2) introducing uncertainty indicators to boost user confidence. Our results indicate that both approaches significantly increase click-through rates. This work offers empirical insights into click behavior on PSI and provides actionable recommendations for search engines aiming to improve their services.

Personalized search engines, which utilize a user's browsing history to tailor web page rankings, have seen rapid growth in recent years. However, this practice raises privacy concerns, as it involves monitoring user activity across multiple websites. This paper presents a framework to quantify the privacy risks of such engines and experimentally demonstrates that current methods fail to sufficiently protect user privacy. Specifically, we show that an attacker can infer sensitive information, such as a user's political preferences, by analyzing personalized search data. To address these issues, we propose two novel privacy-preserving search engine architectures. We evaluated these new designs by measuring both user privacy and search effectiveness. Our evaluations confirm that our proposed solutions significantly reduce the identified privacy risks.

This paper introduces a synthesis system that integrates text and visual inputs to define target programs. Our methodology combines two key strategies: using both visuals and free text to create a more comprehensive description of the desired program, and applying an information retrieval technique that retrieves relevant snippets from a library of example programs to assist in generation. In this setup, the synthesized code must match a given specification by passing a series of automated checks, known as "oracles." We evaluated our approach by having users define target programs using various input combinations, then comparing the generated programs against the intended ones to assess accuracy and robustness across different input modalities. The results indicate that combining text and visuals significantly enhances the system's ability to correctly synthesize programs compared to using either input type alone. Furthermore, our proposed framework successfully synthesized 70% of the target programs within a 10-minute limit on a dataset of 100 target programs, achieving performance that complements existing synthesis frameworks. This work was developed as a participant contribution for the 2021 Synthesis Challenge. The code is available at: https://github.com/SEIS-Lab/SEIS.

7, 2017, from the binary neutron star merger GW170817, along with the associated electromagnetic signals, offers a unique opportunity to examine the equation of state for dense nuclear matter. This study employs the effective field theory of heavy quarks to construct phenomenological models of dense matter, which are then utilized within stochastic gravitational wave waveform models to analyze the inspiral signals of compact binary mergers. Our findings indicate that the high signal-to-noise ratio expected for GW170817 allows us to distinguish between different equations of state. Specifically, the data can rule out soft equations of state characterized by radii smaller than 11.8 km for a 1.4 solar mass neutron star. Furthermore, we observe that the maximum mass limit for non-rotating neutron stars can be set at 2.16 solar masses, a value that remains robust against variations in the specific form of the heavy quark effective field theory. These results demonstrate that the theoretical framework of heavy quarks in dense environments is compatible with the mass-radius constraints derived from gravitational wave observations. Consequently, this suggests that future gravitational wave detections will be capable of distinguishing among various equations of state for dense nuclear matter. Finally, we note that the most stringent rule-out for soft equations of state can be achieved by assuming the presence of a 2.05 solar mass neutron star within the GW170817 source population. Such a constraint would allow us to differentiate between soft equations of state and those that are marginally consistent with current limits. The implications of these findings for the heavy quark effective theory of dense matter are also discussed. The code used in this analysis is available at: https://github.com/ChenYi-NUAA/ETFE-Tidal. This paper demonstrates the application of compositional data analysis to a significant challenge in petroleum engineering: determining the oil, water, and gas saturation levels in porous media during three-phase flow. Because these saturations are compositional in nature, standard linear models fail when applied directly to the raw data. Instead, we utilize log-ratio transformations to convert the data into a format compatible with Euclidean distance and conventional statistical techniques. Following this transformation, principal component analysis (PCA) is performed to identify the primary sources of variability within the dataset. The resulting PCA scores are then used to construct a linear regression model that effectively predicts one component from the others. The study validates the method using both experimental and numerical data, revealing a high correlation between predicted and actual water saturation values across the range of 0.2 to 0.8. Furthermore, the study offers an interpretation of the compositional PCA applied to the numerical dataset, illustrating how the first principal component distinguishes between water and gas as the dominant fluid under specific flow conditions. Finally, an analysis of the method's limitations within a compositional framework is provided. Overall, our findings indicate that principal component analysis and linear regression are powerful tools for efficiently analyzing large volumes of compositional data in chemical and mechanical flow problems, offering a promising avenue for future research. Furthermore, the application of these techniques to reduce data dimensionality before feeding it into machine learning models represents a highly promising direction for subsequent work. While a direct link between these MBHs and star formation in their host galaxies remains elusive, a significant anti-correlation exists between the AGN-to-X-ray luminosity ratio and the specific star formation rate (sSFR). This suggests that highly star-forming galaxies may suppress MBH accretion, a phenomenon potentially explained by the co-evolution of MBHs and stars via galaxy-scale gas outflows. This study investigates the relationship between MBH accretion and galactic outflows using a large dataset of 1,300 RL AGN (with 0.1 < z < 2.5) from the Chandra Deep Field South, cross-referenced with the COSMOS2015 catalog to obtain precise optical photometry and physical properties. We identified a "broad-line" (BL) AGN sub-sample, characterized by broad emission lines from the broad-line region (BLR), which exhibits lower sSFRs compared to non-BL AGN. Furthermore, we analyzed MBH accretion in galaxies with sSFRs below and above 10$^{-11}$ yr$^{-1}$, finding that BL AGN reside in low-sSFR galaxies and tend to have higher Eddington ratios ($\lambda_{\rm Edd}$) than non-BL AGN within the same sSFR regime. These findings indicate that MBH accretion is most efficient in galaxies with sSFRs lower than 10$^{-11}$ yr$^{-1}$, and that MBHs in high-sSFR galaxies may be prevented from accreting due to the momentum transfer from intense star formation. Additionally, the results suggest that MBH accretion is more efficient in galaxies hosting BLR-emitting gas. Finally, we observed that BLR gas kinematics are more turbulent in high-sSFR galaxies, implying that the momentum transfer from stars to the MBH is more effective in suppressing accretion in these systems. These conclusions align with the "galactic wind" model of MBH co-evolution. This research will be published in The Astrophysical Journal. (Abridged)

While often driven by a desire for clarity, precision, or relevance, such posts can also stem from laziness or a lack of effort. Although detrimental to the community, the high visibility of top-voted popular questions might encourage new users to begin with them, potentially skewing the site's question distribution. Searching for relevant content is a critical first step in knowledge creation, yet it is frequently overlooked. New users on Stack Overflow often fail to locate existing answers, leading to the duplication of questions. To address this, we aim to identify the causes of these redundant posts and suggest solutions. We analyzed a dataset of 1.5 million questions, discovering that 15% are derivative, meaning they reuse popular questions as seeds. By analyzing question titles, we developed a method to detect derivative questions with 88% accuracy. This detection reveals that derivative questions are more likely to occur in underrepresented technology areas, receive fewer upvotes, and generate fewer comments. To improve the Stack Overflow experience, we recommend conducting a search tutorial and automatically down-voting derivative questions to discourage their creation.

Derivative questions, which reuse popular questions as seeds, are common on Stack Overflow, with 15% of all questions falling into this category. These posts often duplicate value by asking what has already been answered, yet they can be insightful if they extend previous answers with new details. This paper investigates the characteristics of derivative questions to help distinguish between duplications and extensions. We introduced a technique to identify these questions by measuring text similarity between a candidate question and a "seed" question, achieving 88% accuracy. Our analysis indicates that derivative questions are more prevalent in less common technology areas, receive fewer upvotes, and generate fewer comments. These insights can guide Stack Overflow in reducing unnecessary questions while retaining those with added value. Finally, we discuss various interventions, including a search tutorial and reputation adjustments, designed to minimize the creation of derivative questions.

In recent years, the proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has created new opportunities for attackers to launch large-scale attacks by exploiting vulnerabilities in individual machines. Consequently, there is an urgent need to enhance defense mechanisms for securing IoT networks. This study proposes a method to bolster security by analyzing network traffic and comparing it against a theoretical model of the system. We developed a reverse engineering tool that reconstructs a system's behavior from network traffic, creating an approximate model that, while not perfectly accurate, captures essential features. This model serves as a baseline to flag suspicious activities that deviate from normal operation. Our implementation was tested on real devices running various services, including web servers, databases, and web browsers. Experimental results demonstrate that our technique can identify attacks with a detection rate of 90%. Additionally, we have released the source code for our tool as an open-access repository.
