This study investigates how generalizations of parity, or $O(d)$ symmetry, enable correct two-particle statistics in two spatial dimensions without relying on the fractional statistics typically assumed there. By employing topological arguments, we demonstrate that parity S-matrices corresponding to bosonic and fermionic representations are consistently defined and analytic specifically in two-dimensional space. Utilizing these generalizations, we construct wavefunctions with bosonic and fermionic statistics across two-dimensional spaces for particle pairs where individual particle statistics remain undefined. Constructing these two-dimensional generalizations requires non-trivial, representation-dependent analytic properties within two extra dimensions. Consequently, we establish a link between the construction of such generalizations in two spatial dimensions and certain hypergeometric functions, as well as their connection to conformal field theory in three spatial dimensions. Finally, we provide examples of consistently defined generalizations in two spatial dimensions for boson and fermion pairs and outline methods to derive their counterparts in three spatial dimensions. This approach represents the first attempt to build generalizations of parity that correctly implement quantum statistics, a concept that holds significant relevance for developing multi-particle quantum theories based on higher-spin particles. The latter theory is anticipated to be a variant of the Bagger-Lambert-Gustavsson theory. The derived generalizations of parity may also assist in resolving the long-standing problem of defining the spin-statistics connection for higher-spin particles. The latter topic remains an open question, as the standard generalization of the spin-statistics theorem currently exists only in three spatial dimensions. The construction of these generalizations may also be relevant to recent efforts to formulate generalizations of spin-statistics that correctly implement higher-spin particle statistics. The topological nature of parity S-matrices suggests that similar topological techniques could be applied to develop generalizations of the spin-statistics connection for higher-spin particles. Furthermore, the analytic properties of the bosonic and fermionic parity S-matrices in two spatial dimensions allow for the definition of a branch cut connecting the bosonic and fermionic limits, a feature that may hold significance for recent attempts to generalize the spin-statistics connection. The topological character of these generalizations also holds relevance for the recently proposed generalization of the spin-statistics connection. This is because the proposed method for implementing bosonic and fermionic statistics for higher-spin particles relies on the parity S-matrix, which is known to exist in three spatial dimensions. We first examine the limitations of the original RingCT design, specifically its vulnerability to targeted attacks, and then present our modified protocol alongside a detailed proof of its security properties. Our approach substitutes the set of signers in a RingCT commitment with a delegation structure inspired by practical designated delegation schemes in proof-of-work systems. This scheme permits signers to generate partial signatures, which can be combined to form a complete partial signature; this is known as practical delegated authorization. The proposed scheme maintains a linear relationship between signature size and computational cost, a feature linear delegated authorization schemes lack. Furthermore, our scheme ensures the security of partial and recombination authorizations under the q-eCDH assumption. Finally, the security of practical delegated authorization in our scheme relies on the (standard) CDH assumption. Our scheme offers several benefits, including reduced signature lengths and sizes, and efficiency gains in terms of time and computational resources. Finally, we evaluated the performance of our scheme against other schemes in practical delegated authorization. The results indicate that Delegated RingCT is approximately 2.33 times faster than the original RingCT scheme. The source code is available at https://github.com/Monero-project/monero.

We demonstrate that ensemble members typically possess highly non-random graph features, such as specific subgraph counts, which converge to their expected values slowly. Furthermore, a significant portion of this variance can be attributed to a few "Cayley" codes, a specialized subclass with a rigorous mathematical definition. These Cayley codes exhibit substantially lower degrees of freedom (DOF) than the ensemble average and display consistently superior error correction capabilities. Our findings suggest a novel approach to LDPC code design: instead of relying on random ensembles, one should identify low-DOF subset members that possess favorable traits. We illustrate this strategy by applying it to identify high-quality LDPC codes within the Gallager D ensemble. This methodology is broadly applicable and has already yielded excellent results for binary erasure channel (BEC) ensemble members discovered by our group. Additionally, we outline a general framework for evaluating the quality of LDPC ensembles, utilizing this to analyze ensemble members, the Cayley code subset, and other specialized categories. Ultimately, we advocate for shifting the LDPC code design paradigm from ensemble-based selection to subset-based identification. This approach not only uncovers high-quality codes but also offers a deeper understanding of the underlying structures of these codes. Finally, we anticipate that this strategy will prove valuable for other coding schemes, including convolutional codes.

This study aims to introduce such a framework by addressing three core inquiries: 1) Can in-context learning be achieved without training? 2) What mechanisms enable it? 3) What are its primary limitations? By integrating empirical observations with theoretical analysis, we offer preliminary answers to these questions. First, our findings indicate that in-context learning does not necessitate traditional training; instead, it emerges from the architecture of implicit attention mechanisms within transformer models. Second, we propose a novel theoretical perspective demonstrating that large-scale pre-trained models inherently function as next-word prediction dictionaries, while the implicit attention mechanism allows for dynamic, data-driven selection of these predictions based on specific inputs. Third, inherent constraints of the implicit attention mechanism and the dictionary-based nature of pre-trained models limit the scalability of in-context learning. Collectively, our theoretical analysis and empirical results suggest that the success of in-context learning is an unintended consequence of the transformer's design and the pre-training process of modern language models. Consequently, this work paves the way for unleashing the adaptability of large-scale language models without training by exploring in-context learning and transfer. Finally, our theoretical model establishes a new paradigm for investigating the learnability of in-context learning. the lepton sector has been a significant pursuit, with the most promising system for discovering new physics being the neutral heavy lepton, or neutrino. This study examines a model featuring a right-handed neutrino, which is a primary motivation for the Muon $g-2$ experiment. We calculate the contribution of the neutral heavy lepton to $C\!P$ violation in the muon's electric dipole moment (EDM). Our analysis demonstrates that the magnitude of the muon EDM serves as a reliable probe for the parameter $\sin\phi_{\mu h} \equiv \sin\phi$, where $\phi$ denotes the phase difference between the couplings of the lightest Higgs bosion to fermions and gauge bosons. Specifically, the contribution to the muon EDM is proportional to the product of the couplings of the lightest Higgs boson to the muon and the right-handed neutrino, as well as the mixing angle between the neutral heavy lepton and charged leptons. Furthermore, we estimate the contribution to the electron EDM, finding it to be approximately 100 times smaller than that of the muon EDM. Consequently, the electron EDM is unlikely to be detected in the foreseeable future. Finally, we analyze the potential of the Muon $g-2$ experiment to constrain the parameter space, determining that the experiment can probe the product of the couplings of the lightest Higgs boson to the muon and the right-handed neutrino within the range $10^{-3} \lesssim |g_{\mu} g_{N}|\lesssim 10^{-1}$. This corresponds to a reach of approximately $\sin\phi \lesssim 10^{-1}$, assuming lepton flavor violating mixing angles of $10^{-2}$. Our conclusions are illustrated through various plots. Additionally, we estimate the contribution of the right-handed neutrino to the muon anomalous magnetic moment, $a_{\mu}$. We show that the model can address the current discrepancy between the experimental and standard model values of $a_{\mu}$, provided that $\sin\phi \lesssim 10^{-1}$. This scenario is viable if the couplings of the lightest Higgs boson to the muon and right-handed neutrino fall within the range $10^{-2} \lesssim |g_{\mu} g_{N}|\lesssim 10^{-1}$.

# 1. Introduction

Artificial speech production holds significant value across various fields, including the creation of new voice data for ASR and TTS, voice cloning, and the generation of accentual and emotional variations. Traditionally, these tasks have been accomplished using transfer learning or style transfer methods, which necessitate collecting data for a target voice and defining a reference style. Although recent advancements in style transfer allow for the creation of arbitrary styles from a single input, they still depend on the selection of an appropriate target voice.

In this work, we present a system capable of generating speech styles and accents that were neither present in nor related to the original speaker's data. By removing the transfer phase entirely, our approach enables the instant creation of novel voice styles and accents without any additional data collection. This capability opens up new avenues for research, such as producing entirely alien or fantastical voices. Additionally, the system facilitates the synthesis of speech styles that do not exist in the source data, which is vital for enhancing speech rendering in speech rendering and compression tasks. In contrast, the topological approach identifies universal features that remain independent of specific details, such as the shape of the driving field. This chapter initially outlines both methodologies using a coherent quantum two-level system as a case study, subsequently applying the topological perspective to elucidate key principles governing more complex multiwell systems. We analyze how the initial intensity of vertical or horizontal magnetic fields, as well as the rotation rate, affects cloud formation. Our results indicate that when rotation is strong, both vertical and horizontal magnetic fields significantly suppress the development of dense gas, whereas in non-rotating conditions, their influence varies substantially by orientation. Specifically, a moderate initial vertical magnetic field consistently hinders density enhancement, while a moderate horizontal field does not, though a strong horizontal field eventually suppresses it similarly to the vertical case. These findings offer insights into the early evolution of protoplanetary disks and the magnetic fields surrounding young stellar objects. We conclude that rotation combined with a moderate horizontal magnetic field promotes the fragmentation of turbulent flows, which is essential for creating the inhomogeneous density structures observed in protoplanetary disks. This supports the hypothesis that small-scale magnetic fields generate anisotropic stresses, driving the radial transport of angular momentum in these disks. Finally, we propose that this mechanism could explain the origin of the "accretion dead zone" seen around young stars. The presented model offers a potential framework for understanding the complex relationship between stellar accretion rates and the properties of the embedded protostars within protoplanetary disk systems. This study is part of the project "Formation of Planetary Systems," which is part of the Planetary Science Decadal Plan in South Korea. The research was conducted using the K-Cloud code, a domestic supercomputer developed by the Korea Astronomy and Space Science Institute (KASI). K-Cloud offers an integrated environment for simulating various astrophysical phenomena, including star and planet formation, supernovae, and gamma-ray bursts. It features a suite of physical modules, such as those for magnetohydrodynamics, multi-dimensional gravity, and radiative transfer, all of which are crucial for modeling star and planet formation. The K-Cloud code includes a new adaptive mesh refinement (AMR) algorithm designed to efficiently resolve steep gradients in density and temperature. Additionally, it incorporates a new time-parallelization strategy to enable the efficient simulation of large-scale star and planet formation scenarios. large-scale networks of homogeneous agents. By employing a nonlinear scalar push-pull architecture, we demonstrate that, provided per-agent interactions remain bounded, network-wide activity can be sustained at any desired level below saturation by adjusting two distinct parameters. The first parameter governs the global activity magnitude, while the second modulates the level of heterophily—the degree to which agents possess distinct preferences—within the system.

Empirically, we observe a trade-off between mean squared error (MSE) and the mean pairwise preference alignment metric, denoted as $\rho$. We numerically establish that, in the limit of large networks, these two metrics interact according to a hyperbolic relationship. Leveraging this hyperbolic model, we identify the optimal conditions for agent design to achieve a target balance between low MSE and high alignment, thereby maximizing both simultaneously.

Furthermore, we extend this framework to multi-class multi-preference scenarios, maintaining bounded interactions. In this context, we prove that the hyperbolic relationship between MSE and mean pairwise preference alignment remains valid, even when agents adhere to a Gaussian distribution of preferences. This extension offers a method to determine optimal class representatives that optimize both MSE and the pairwise alignment between arbitrary agent classes.

Finally, we apply this model to the multi-preference multi-class FGL framework, analyzing how well it approximates the optimal equilibrium between performance and alignment. Our numerical results indicate that, although the scalar push-pull approach is a coarse approximation, it successfully captures the fundamental trade-off between low MSE and high preference alignment. This confirms the model's utility in achieving near-optimal agent designs.

To achieve this, we employ the sample variance within a robust confidence interval for the regression's quantile function. This interval is designed to maintain a specific level of confidence even when a proportion $p$ of the data is contaminated. This approach can be extended to other models featuring a location parameter, offering a method to create a confidence region for that parameter resistant to outliers, provided the interval maintains validity even with identical values substituted for the $p$ corrupted observations. The core technique involves utilizing the sample variance in a robust interval for the model's quantile function, ensuring it remains effective despite contamination. By analyzing a specific outlier model, we derive a closed-form expression for the interval's length, which is subsequently applied to various outlier detection and error correction contexts. The primary advantage of this method is its dependence on bounded variance; unlike many alternative techniques, it does not require asymptotic normality of errors or $n$-th order moments. Furthermore, the method remains effective even when the $p$-fraction of corrupted data is as high as 0.30. Error correction applications demonstrate how to leverage this outlier identification process to enhance error correction capabilities. Finally, we examine the method's performance under other models by testing its application to interval estimation for a location parameter in a univariate median model. The resulting interval is robust to both corrupted and non-corrupted data, with a calculated breakdown point. Error correction applications illustrate how to improve error correction by combining this interval with an outlier model. In this context, the interval estimates a parameter by fitting a line to a contaminated dataset using the sample median instead of the mean, and we determine the necessary conditions for this error correction to function. We also establish bounds on the error coverage probability, proving that the method's performance is unaffected by the distribution of uncorrupted data or the specific locations of corrupted data points. Additionally, we derive bounds on the error coverage probability for the case where $p=0$. Error correction applications prove that the interval can error-correct up to $p(n-1)/2$ errors, with performance improving as $p$ increases. We further bound the probability that the interval fails to include the true parameter value, proving that this probability approaches zero as $n$ increases, regardless of the error distribution. While historically constrained by physical constraints like wireless propagation delays and on-board computing time, this trend can now be addressed by offloading processing to ground stations. Although this approach introduces new challenges—such as transmitting raw data over potentially unreliable downlink connections and managing multiple, possibly uncooperative satellites—it becomes a viable solution when reliable communications are guaranteed. This paper demonstrates the effectiveness of this ground-dependent strategy using the CubeSat drag de-orbit experiment (CDDEx) as a case study. CDDEx involves releasing test payloads from low-Earth orbit CubeSat buses at predefined times to study the effects of initial burnup conditions on these test units. The test buses are equipped with ground-dependent downlinks that provide both higher bandwidth and more reliable communications than ungrounded downlinks. By utilizing these downlinks to rapidly transmit in-flight data for immediate analysis, the experiment team can determine the precise moment to initiate payload release. This capability significantly enhances the experiment's accuracy and demonstrates the broader potential of ground-dependent downlinks to support time-critical data processing for future missions. To facilitate the adaptation of this method for other scientific objectives, the authors have shared the necessary software tools and code repositories. Ultimately, this work underscores that ground-dependent downlinks offer increased flexibility for high-frequency data transmission and real-time processing, thereby expanding the range of achievable experimental outcomes. The sharing of these tools aims to enable the future scientific community to efficiently and effectively conduct their own ground-dependent experiments.

Our primary objective is the development of an AI-driven framework for creating synthetic human driving trajectories to bolster autonomous vehicle (AV) systems. This framework comprises two primary modules: a driving behavior generator and an adversarial generator. The driving behavior module produces human driving patterns using recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) units, while the adversarial component seeks to refine the parameters of the driving behavior generator by minimizing the discrepancy between generated and actual driving trajectories. To facilitate this adversarial process, we introduce a novel loss function that quantifies the deviation between predicted and observed trajectories. Trained on a comprehensive dataset of 10,000 human driving trajectories, our model achieves high fidelity in reproducing human driving behaviors, as evidenced by substantial reductions in both Logarithmic Loss (LL) and Continuous Conditional Inception Score (CCIS). These capabilities hold significant promise for enhancing the safety and efficacy of autonomous driving systems. Our code and data are available at https://github.com/andrewandrews/Adversarial-Driving-Generation.

For any orthonormal basis $\mathcal{B}$ of $H$, the set of coefficients $\{ \langle Tx, x \rangle : x \in \mathcal{B} \}$ forms a sequence in $\mathbb{C}$, which we denote as $\omega(T, \mathcal{B})$. Given a closed subset $K \subset \mathbb{C}$, an operator $T$ is defined as $K$-quasinilpotent if $\omega(T, \mathcal{B}) \subset K$ for every orthonormal basis $\mathcal{B}$. This paper investigates this class by addressing the following questions: (Q1) Is $\mathcal{Q}(K)$ closed in the norm topology? (Q2) Is $\mathcal{Q}(K)$ weakly closed? We formulate the CSMA packet capture probability, mean system delay, and throughput probability as functions of the ramp-up time, cut-off threshold, and interference bandwidth. Through simulation, we compare these mean values against those achieved by OR- and ALOHA-based methods, demonstrating that the proposed CSMA approach superiorly minimizes mean system delay and maximize throughput probability. Furthermore, we establish that these mechanisms yield optimal performance when a ratio of approximately $10\text{--}20$ dB exists between the ramp-up time and the ramp-down time. Numerical results indicate that the proposed CSMA protocol outperforms both traditional CSMA and OR methods in terms of mean system delay and throughput probability. This superior performance is realized when the ramp-up time and cut-off threshold are set to at least $1.5$ and $2.0$ times the radar signal's observation time, respectively. Finally, we show that the proposed CSMA protocol outperforms ALOHA and OR methods when the ramp-up time and cut-off threshold exceed $10$ and $20$ times the observation time, respectively. This performance advantage holds true even when the cut-off threshold is lower than the interference bandwidth. The proposed protocol is applicable to existing FMCW radar systems, such as those used in automotive applications. This is accomplished by adjusting the ramp-up time, cut-off threshold, and observation time of the FMCW radar signal to align with the desired performance metrics. This flexibility allows the protocol to effectively address the interference challenges posed by existing FMCW radar systems. This work details a novel method for generating such entangled spatial-photon pairs, achieved by illuminating a q-plate with a superposition of fundamental (l=0) and higher-order (l=l+1, l-l+1) Laguerre-Gaussian (LG) modes. These properties can be readily detected using a spatial mode sorter or a spiral phase plate (SPP) combined with a single-camera OAM mode multiplexer. The resulting entangled states are mathematically expressed as combinations of four OAM terms (+l, -l, +2l, -2l) or eight OAM terms ranging from -3l to +3l. We demonstrate the detection of these entangled states using a compact spatial mode sorter and propose their characterization via quantum tomography. Furthermore, we show that the visibility of entanglement can be enhanced by adjusting the power ratio between the input LG modes. These findings offer a promising new approach for generating entangled spatial-photon pairs, which could significantly benefit quantum communication and computing applications. Additionally, this method provides a viable pathway for experimentally studying the interaction between spatial and OAM degrees of freedom within spatial-mode multiplexed (squared) systems. Finally, these entangled states serve as valuable resources for implementing quantum protocols, including quantum key distribution, quantum teleportation, and the demonstration of Bell nonlocality. Moreover, they can be readily extended to higher-order entangled states by incorporating more than two LG modes into the input superposition. This research establishes a foundation for the continued development of spatial-mode multiplexed quantum systems. This paper investigates how an impacting object's vibration, ground sound, and the coupling effect jointly influence the resulting acoustic signal. To achieve this, we introduce a novel synthesis framework comprising three modular modules: an auto-encoding model for impact tone generation, a ground sound module, and an additive acoustic coupling module. This investigation relies on examining stationary dynamics on the character space of the amenable radical, specifically proving stiffness by demonstrating that every stationary probability measure remains invariant. This finding extends a classical theorem by Furstenberg regarding dynamics on the torus. Furthermore, assuming a higher rank condition, we demonstrate that any action on the character space of a finitely generated virtually nilpotent group exhibits stiffness. Our primary methodology involves reducing dynamical problems to spectral ones and utilizing compactness arguments grounded in a novel characterization of characters for linear virtually nilpotent groups, which generalizes a result by Steinberg. While various design approaches exist, this paper introduces a novel architecture for the fail-operational level tailored for automated driving. The proposed design employs two driving computers, each protected by two Memory Protection Units (MPUs). These computing modules exchange data via Ethernet, with the communication channel monitored by a cross-check computer consisting of three replicas without mutual redundancy. Simulation results demonstrate the viability of the proposed architecture, and a hardware prototype has also been developed to validate fail-operational behavior. The study evaluates the effectiveness of two neural network-based methods for detecting and localizing faults in automated driving systems. First, a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) was trained on fault data to identify anomalies in video streams from external sensors. Second, a recurrent neural network was utilized to identify inconsistencies in the outputs of automated driving functions. Testing was conducted using data from simulated faulty driving scenarios. Results indicate that both approaches successfully detected and localized specific fault types. A preliminary hardware prototype confirmed the practical feasibility of utilizing effective driving computers and external sensor systems to achieve multiple layers of fault monitoring. These findings suggest that deep learning techniques can be effectively applied to monitor various failure modes, including hardware malfunctions and software bugs, within automated driving systems.

In the context of automated driving, sensor systems are critical for perceiving the vehicle's surroundings. To ensure safety, these sensors must be continuously monitored to identify malfunctions. This paper proposes a monitoring architecture using redundant sensors, where each unit is individually analyzed by a neural network to detect anomalies. Furthermore, the consistency among the sensors is regularly evaluated to pinpoint individual faulty units. To validate the feasibility of this approach, a hardware prototype was developed and tested. The authors concluded that multiple monitoring layers are essential for comprehensive fault detection and that the proposed architecture successfully achieves this goal.

The core challenge lies in creating a monitor that is both faithful to the original code and robust against runtime exceptions. While a faithful (or transparent) monitor must precisely implement the specification without introducing new behavior, a robust (or opaque) monitor must be exception-free even if that means deviating from the specification. Although several approaches exist for both scenarios, this work focuses exclusively on the robust method. We propose a new automatic technique that enhances clarity by separating the code into two distinct parts: conditions and actions. The method prioritizes the specification of exceptions within the conditions, ensuring that exception handling occurs before any other actions. This approach eliminates the need for complex control-flow analysis, thereby reducing algorithmic complexity and improving the clarity of the resulting dual program. We validate this proposal using a benchmark suite of 20 cases. Our findings indicate that, compared to previous techniques, the generated monitors are more faithful to the input, exhibit lower exception density, and offer a more precise characterization of the impacts resulting from the adoption of robustness. This benchmark suite is publicly available at: https://bit.ly/3iWl20s. The proposed technique and its evaluation are also detailed in the journal article by M. J. Serrano, J. Armin, and F. The entrance of the nanofiber functions as a bundle emission source, where the output intensity profile is dictated by the spatial arrangement of the constituent emitters. For a single emitter, the bundle exhibits robust polarization-preserving robustness, maintaining the input polarization across the entire transverse section without distortion, regardless of the number of components or the transverse mode distribution. When two quantum emitters are aligned parallel to one another, the system generates cross-polarized correlation photons at the nanofiber tip, with correlation strength contingent upon their relative spacing. In contrast, arranging the emitters perpendicular to each other results in the collection of polarized correlation photons matching the input polarization. Perpendicular configurations also enable the creation of super-pseudo entangled states, achieving higher brightness than parallel setups. Furthermore, these perpendicular arrangements facilitate the bundle emission of high-dimensional qudit entangled photons, with dimensionality determined by the emitters' spatial positions. The underlying physics of this quantum behavior is elucidated through a quantum circuit model, intensity simulations, and correlation analysis. This work demonstrates that both the network topology of the quantum emitter array and the transverse profile of the nanofiber are critical factors in harnessing the potential of quantum bundle sources. The proposed approach offers a versatile platform for generating high-energy, high-dimensional network quantum resources at the network entrance while preserving the underlying quantum correlations. This methodology holds significant promise for scalable and practical applications in quantum information processing. The theoretical framework presented here may also extend to other multi-emitter quantum systems, such as those based on quantum dots or atoms integrated into cold atom networks. These higher multipoles amplify the backreaction on lower orders and can drastically alter the gravitational interaction between two binary black holes (BBHs) as they approach. This study examines the effect of such higher multipoles on BBHs using a post-Newtonian (PN) framework. We demonstrate that the conservative mass shift of a BBH scales with the product of its multipole moments, whereas radiative mass and spin shifts depend on the sum of pairs multiplied by a third moment. Our findings indicate that higher multipoles can cause a substantial increase in the time required for a BBH binary to merge. Additionally, these multipoles generate substantial shifts in both radiative mass and spin, suggesting that a BBH's apparent mass and spin can remain in significant disagreement with post-collision post-Newtonian predictions for extended periods. Finally, we observe that these post-Newtonian effects on merge time are comparable to known numerical errors in current post-Newtonian models, implying that neglecting higher multipoles may limit the achievable order of post-Newtonian theory. This suggests a potential avenue for reducing numerical uncertainty by incorporating higher multipole contributions into the post-Newtonian formalism. To support this approach, we provide an appendix listing the post-Newtonian expressions for BBH mass, spin, and spin precession frequency that include contributions from various multipoles. Furthermore, we note that similar multipole effects are expected in other scenarios, such as planets orbiting stars, where they could influence the evolution of orbital parameters. In this context, we provide a simple post-Newtonian estimate of the gravitational multipole induced by a planet orbiting a star. Finally, we briefly discuss the implications of these findings for interpreting post-merger data from the LIGO/Virgo/KAGRA observatories. P4 is the dominant language for defining rules in modern programmable network switches, valued for its ability to accept an unlimited number of rules with diverse header fields and actions. However, this openness introduces potential verification issues, including incomplete network coverage, redundant rules, and conflicts. While existing verification tools rely on static analysis of compiled P4 binaries, they often fail to detect conflicts that only manifest under specific traffic patterns. Conversely, dynamic testing methods are ineffective because they cannot explore the full range of possible traffic patterns. This work proposes a new approach to P4 verification by formally modeling both the P4 program and its network semantics in Coq. This enables the automatic derivation of a verification condition that encapsulates all possible traffic patterns, which is then discharged using a combination of SMT solvers and a custom tool. Consequently, this method achieves a form of dynamic verification that is independent of specific traffic patterns. We have implemented a tool capable of taking a P4 program along with its compiled JSON and BM2 binaries and automatically verifying it in under a minute. Using this implementation, we have verified 40 P4 programs from the OpenP4 collection, confirming that none contain language coverage issues, duplicate rules

This requirement divides admissible element-wise vector fields into two categories: those that conserve mass within each element and those that do not. The latter category includes functions that can improve the global mass conservation of a vector field through the addition of scalar degrees of freedom, effectively acting as pressure modes. ### 1. Introduction

The etching of grating structures into silicon using an inductively coupled plasma (ICP) is a widely employed technique for fabricating optical components, such as grating couplers for integrated photonics. Due to the inherent non-linearity of the etching process, the sidewalls of the resulting structures often exhibit re-entrant profiles, meaning the width changes non-monotonically as a function of depth. While these re-entrant features can adversely affect the performance of optical devices, they also present an opportunity to exploit the phenomenon for multi-step grating etching. In this current study, we investigate the origins of oscillations in the width profile and propose a simple explanation for their occurrence. This phenomenon was previously documented in a study where the authors attributed the oscillations to a complex interaction between the plasma etching process and the grating's geometry. In this work, we replicate the findings of that previous study and show how the reported simple explanation for oscillations can account for the oscillatory width profile. Our results indicate that oscillations are a natural outcome of the etching process, arising from the re-use of grating features across multiple planes. To simulate realistic movement, we design the snake to execute a sinusoidal motion. Furthermore, we develop collision detection and response mechanisms to enable the snake to navigate around obstacles. Finally, we present a simulation in which the snake successfully traverses a maze. The source code for this project is accessible online. Our work can also be viewed on the featured demo platform.

The world contains numerous creatures, some of which can climb walls. To represent this, we model a spider and a frog, with plans to include more in future updates. These animals move using multiple limbs, a characteristic shared by many species. This multi-limbed mobility is crucial for their ability to scale vertical surfaces.

To render climbing behavior realistic, we employ a snake-like approach. Snakes are ideal for this dynamic because, despite lacking limbs, they move using multiple points of contact with the ground. This parallels the multi-limbed strategy of climbers like the spider and frog. Our goal is to create a unified method for simulating movement that can be applied to creatures with or without limbs.

Our approach models the creature as a chain of connected joints, where each segment acts as a rigid body. To ensure smooth motion, we configure the snake to perform a sinusoidal movement. We have implemented a comprehensive collision detection and response system to allow the snake to navigate obstacles. A maze traversal simulation demonstrates the effectiveness of our method.

This study introduces a two-stage deep reinforcement learning framework designed to optimize electric energy storage and release. The approach is divided into policy initialization and fine-tuning phases. During initialization, the problem is decomposed into a state estimation task and a policy initialization task. State estimation utilizes a deep neural network to extract features from raw observations, while the policy is pre-trained using policy gradient methods based on these estimated states. The fine-tuning phase then jointly optimizes the deep state estimator and the policy using actor-critic algorithms. Evaluations on a real-world dataset from a 500kV transmission line demonstrate that this framework reduces the total cost of electric energy imbalance by 40% compared to the traditional DQN method. Furthermore, the proposed solution requires 50% less training time than current state-of-the-art approaches. The approach's efficacy is validated by its robust performance and computational efficiency across two real-world datasets with varying sample sizes. These findings indicate that the proposed solution serves as a robust, data-driven framework for efficiently optimizing energy balance in transmission power stations. This paper introduces the concept of predicting out-of-distribution (OOD) results, drawing an analogy from physics regarding phase transitions. We illustrate the advantages of the OOD approach through a case study of the 2020 COVID-19 outbreak in the United States, utilizing a data-driven model based on a fourth-order polynomial. The analysis targets a specific class of LLPs capable of decaying into two b-quark jets, with a minimum decay product energy threshold of 100 GeV. Data collected in 2015 and 2016 were combined, yielding a combined integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. A displaced Higgs boson decaying into two b-quark jets ($H\rightarrow b\bar{b}$) serves as a primary reference signal. No significant excess above the standard model background was observed. Consequently, 95% confidence level exclusion limits were established for various signal regions, covering models such as supersymmetry and long-lived vector quarkonia, for scenarios involving two b-quark jets with transverse energies exceeding 100 GeV. These limits are presented as a function of the signal's cross section multiplied by the branching ratio into displaced b-jet pairs, based on the number of b-tagged jets in the final state. The smallest cross section times branching ratio into displaced b-b pairs at a 95% C.L. is 0.01 pb for a jet pair invariant mass of 115 GeV, and 0.005 pb for a mass of 91 GeV. For a two-jet final state with an average displacement of 10 cm, the corresponding lifetime upper limits are 0.14 and 0.07, respectively. Similarly, upper limits of 0.03 and 0.02 were derived for jets with an average transverse displacement of 1 meter for the 115 and 91 GeV mass cases, respectively. These findings offer the most stringent constraints to date for long-lived particles decaying into b-quark pairs with a 91 GeV invariant mass. Furthermore, this is the first search specifically optimized for highly ionizing displaced b-jets, achieving the smallest cross section times the branching ratio into such a final state at a 95% C.L. of 0.001 pb for a two-jet system with an average transverse displacement of 1 meter. However, the specific link between the dynamics arising from vibrations and those originating from the energy landscape remains unclear. This study examines this relationship by comparing the time evolution of the intermediate scattering function, $F_q(t)$, derived from either component in over-dense hard-sphere glasses. Our findings indicate that although neither contribution individually predicts the observed $F_q(t)$, combining both contributions yields excellent agreement with these dynamics. These results strongly suggest that the critical slowing down of hard-sphere glass dynamics arises from a synergistic effect between the energy landscape and the vibrational density of states. Furthermore, we demonstrate that these contributions are multiplexed, meaning they can be switched on or off without altering their relative composition. This capability offers a novel avenue for independently tuning the vibrational and energy landscape contributions to dynamics. Finally, our analysis confirms that the nonexponential nature of $F_q(t)$ in hard-sphere glasses is governed by an interplay between these two contributions, contrary to the view that it stems solely from the energy landscape. These insights provide a foundation for developing a more comprehensive understanding of the dynamic heterogeneities present in glasses. Additionally, we show that the nonexponential behavior of $F_q(t)$ in one-component model glasses can be effectively captured by a single parameter, $\Delta$, which quantifies the degree of heterogeneity. This single-parameter description remains robust across various temperatures and densities. Our results also indicate that the vibrational density of states associated with a given $\Delta$ is universal for all systems exhibiting that specific level of dynamic heterogeneity. These conclusions are supported by comparisons with experiments on real glasses. Furthermore, we demonstrate that vibrational density of states experiments can successfully predict the nonexponentiality of $F_q(t)$ in both hard-sphere and silica glasses. These findings align with a recently proposed universal relationship between structural and dynamic properties in glasses. Collectively, these findings offer a fresh perspective on vibrational density of states experiments and their implications for understanding glass dynamics. These outcomes complement our earlier work on the coupling between vibrational and energy landscape contributions to dynamics [Phys. Rev. E \textbf{97}, 042120 (2018)]. These findings will be presented at the 2019 International Conference on Glasses and Amorphous Materials. This research will also be featured in an upcoming paper. These conclusions will be discussed during the 2019 International Conference on Glasses

This review examines the history of the CMS experiment at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), detailing its design, operation, and significant achievements. The CMS detector has achieved numerous firsts in particle physics, including the discovery of a new heavy resonance named the $W'$ boson (2016), the observation of top quark pair production with bottom quarks (2011), the detection of like-sign tritop pair production (2012), the measurement of the forward-backward asymmetry in top quark pair production (2013), the observation of the associated production of a Higgs boson and a $W$ or $Z$ boson (2016), the measurement of the double associated production of Higgs bosons (2018), and the observation of $Z$-boson decays into muon-antimuon pairs into ultra-peripheral collisions (2020). As we move forward, the CMS collaboration is committed to advancing the frontiers of particle physics by continuing to analyze data from the LHC and preparing for the era of the LHC's high luminosity. To meet these challenges, the detector will undergo a comprehensive upgrade, known as CMS Upgrade II, to maintain its role as a leading tool for discovery at the highest energy scales ever attained in particle physics. This document outlines the current status of the CMS experiment and provides an overview of the upgrade plans for CMS Upgrade II.

This far-side object exhibits nearly identical characteristics to 3C279, including its spectrum, variability, and linearly polarized emission. Given that 3C279 displays a complex core structure with multiple components, we propose that F3C279 represents a distinct physical entity. Our findings suggest that the radio emission originates from a jet with a precessing axis. Furthermore, our data indicate that the jet's opening angle is significantly smaller than the axis' precession angle, a scenario that aligns with the observed radio-to-X-ray spectral break. We conclude that F3C279 and 3C279 are likely two separate sources that have been mistakenly identified as a single source due to the limited angular resolution of current Very Long Baseline Array data. This misidentification could explain the puzzling lack of correlation between the gamma-ray and radio bands observed in 3C279. The precessing jet model offers a straightforward explanation for the source's unusual behavior, including its recent bright gamma-ray flares and extended periods of radio quiescence. Additionally, this model supports the hypothesis that X-ray flares in 3C279 may be linked to gamma-ray activity. Finally, our findings underscore the necessity for higher-resolution Very Long Baseline Array observations to definitively determine whether F3C279 and 3C279 are actually distinct sources.

When preference lists are restricted to specific structures, such as bi-partite or circular lists, efficient polynomial-time algorithms exist to find stable matchings. This study examines the Circular Stable Roommates problem (CSR), which arises when agents possess circular preferences. We demonstrate that CSR cannot be solved in polynomial time unless the polynomial-time hierarchy collapses, a failure that holds even if half of the agents' preference lists are provided as fixed input. Furthermore, we present an $O(n^k)$-time algorithm to determine if a stable matching exists for an instance with $n$ agents and $k$ distinct preference lists, a result that is nearly tight given a lower bound of $k=\Omega(n)$. Additionally, we prove that an efficient parameterization by list length is impossible unless the parameterized Exact Cover problem admits a similar efficient solution. Finally, we analyze the problem's robustness by investigating how minor modifications to agent preferences impact the existence of stable matchings. Specifically, we show that altering any single agent's preference list or modifying one entry across all lists transforms CSR into a problem solvable in polynomial time. These findings extend to other variants with circular list constraints, including the Strong Stable Roommates problem. The circular nature of preferences induces long dependency cycles, complicating stability; however, removing just one edge from each cycle eliminates these obstacles and enables efficient solutions. This suggests that circular stable matching is fundamentally a problem about identifying and disrupting a small number of critical cycles. Consequently, we develop a randomized algorithm with a runtime of $2^{O(n)}\cdot \text{poly}(n)$ to solve CSR, which can be made deterministic with only a quadratic loss in success probability. This approach also offers a significantly faster solution for the Strong Stable Roommates problem. Our methodology relies on modeling preferences as a circular arc graph and constructing a stable matching by identifying and breaking a minimum set of cliques within the graph. We validate this strategy by proving that finding a clique cover of size $k$ is W[1]-hard with respect to $k$, even when all cliques are size two. This work is a full version of a paper previously submitted to ISAAC.

While the Gromov--Hausdorff distance converges uniformly to $1$ as two metric spaces approach infinity in diameter, standard metric space theory does not directly apply to this setting. To address this, we introduce $\Gh$, a restricted subcollection of all metric spaces that serves as a convenient proxy for the entire class. This proxy allows us to demonstrate that the Gromov--Hausdorff distance constitutes a true metric on $\Gh$, enabling the application of standard metric space techniques. Furthermore, $\Gh$ retains all essential properties of metric spaces required to establish that the Gromov--Hausdorff distance is complete and uniformly continuous with respect to diameter. A primary utility of $\Gh$ lies in its compact subsets, which correspond precisely to the relatively compact subsets within the class of all metric spaces. This correspondence facilitates an intuitive proof that any sequence of metric spaces, bounded uniformly in diameter, contains a sequence converging in the Gromov--Hausdorff distance to a limit metric space. This result establishes that the class of all metric spaces, under the Gromov--Hausdorff topology, possesses the property of relative compactness implying compactness. This paper serves as a foundational introduction to the theory of metric spaces, aiming to render the framework of the original monograph more accessible. It concludes with a collection of elementary exercises and a preliminary overview of Cantor's intersection theorem within the context of the Gromov--Hausdorff topology. As a supplementary resource, the authors have also made available the LaTeX source code for a version of this paper enhanced with proofs for all exercises. The primary source code can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/stephanklindahl/metric_spaces}. Additionally, a mirror copy is available at \url{https://www.cs.ubc.ca/~schroder/320/Notes/MetricSpaces.pdf}. Consequently, developing efficient, low-overhead architectural designs is essential for the near-term realization of fault-tolerant quantum computers. This study introduces a new efficient surface code layout derived from the triangular code through a sequence of vertex and edge mergers. Notably, this design maintains a three-neighbour regular structure, similar to both the surface code and the triangular code. The resulting logical qubits are encoded within specific homological cycles of a genus-$g$ surface, where the logical $X$ and $Z$ operators correspond to closed paths on the graph. By employing a specific graph coloring, we derive a fault-tolerant measurement circuit for logical $Z$ that requires only $g+1$ logical CNOT operations. Furthermore, we demonstrate that tailoring the ratios of logical $X$ and $Z$ errors allows for the creation of surface codes exhibiting asymmetric error-correction capabilities. These proposals offer valuable insights for the architectural design of quantum computers utilizing superconducting circuits. Additionally, we have made this proposed surface code available as an open-source software tool called QASM-TCN, accessible at https://github.com/HiroyukiKawaguchi/QASM-TCN. This tool enables the efficient simulation of quantum computers implementing the new surface code.

While previous studies have examined the influence of environmental decoherence on quantum sensors, these models typically treated the sensor as a point particle, overlooking the spatially extended nature of real-world sensors. This approach leverages continuous-variable digital qubit architectures, offering enhanced flexibility in dissipation design compared to discrete-variable systems. Using two- and three-qubit examples, we demonstrate that this method significantly lowers experimental thresholds required to enter the critical regime. This suggests that continuous-qubit hybrid computing could advance various multi-qubit quantum technologies, including quantum simulation, computing, and machine learning.

Continuous-variable quantum computing is emerging as a promising framework for scalable quantum information processing. Recent advancements in circuit quantum electrodynamics have enabled digital qubit schemes, facilitating universal gate synthesis through a quantum Fourier transform, an inverse Crowbar circuit, and a continuous-coupling circuit. This progress paves the way for multi-qubit architectures capable of quantum memory, communication, and computation. These continuous-qubit digital approaches can be integrated with auxiliary continuous-microscopic cavitary modes, which support large-scale critical phenomena suitable for type-II superconducting circuit implementations. This combination establishes a hybrid continuous-qubit digital-quantum computing model.

In this work, we analyze entanglement generation driven by critical phenomena within digital-qubit quantum computers. We introduce an analog component to these systems by exploiting large-coupling critical points in the qubit-cavity interface. Our findings indicate that the multi-qubit critical regime, which drives maximal entanglement generation, is accessible at significantly lower qubit-cavity coupling rates than previously thought. This opens new avenues for critical quantum simulation and a wide range of multi-qubit quantum technologies.

**I. INTRODUCTION**

Quantum technologies utilizing superconducting circuits are rapidly advancing, with multi-qubit processors reaching over 100 physical qubits. These systems offer superior connectivity, allowing every qubit to interact directly with every other qubit. This high connectivity mirrors conditions in matter physics, where all particles interact with one another. Consequently, such multi-body systems are expected to exhibit critical phenomena, where long-range correlations emerge and fluctuations become pronounced. These critical phenomena are widely recognized for enabling maximal entanglement generation in multi-qubit quantum technologies.

The second ingredient for achieving criticality is a large interaction strength between quantum entities. In matter physics, this is often realized via an effective large coupling mediated by an environmental bath. In multi-qubit superconducting quantum technologies, this environment is provided by the cavitary mode, which can be engineered to be large in the microwave domain

This paper introduces a novel DNN structure designed for straightforward training while utilizing a number of non-linearities proportional to the training dataset size. As R&D in nuclear and plasma physics and fusion energy advances, a discussion has emerged among researchers and R&D leaders regarding the most effective strategies for advancing this field. The core issue involves selecting among three distinct technological development pathways. The first, described as the "scientific" approach, involves utilizing large-scale user facilities to gather extensive experimental data for theoretical analysis. The second, termed "engineering," focuses on creating smaller, dedicated testbeds or prototypes specifically designed to evaluate a limited number of technological concepts. The third pathway, labeled "adventurous," consists of integrating smaller fusion devices into larger, multi-purpose plasma or nuclear facilities already dedicated to other research agendas. This paper outlines the primary arguments regarding the various options available for progressing nuclear fusion R&D. It concludes by proposing a framework to assess the strengths and weaknesses of each position, aiming to provide a more objective means of comparing these alternatives. This paper introduces a Python package, `pymulti`, designed to facilitate the fitting of multilevel models to trial-level data. This paper introduces a fault-tolerant HPC system built upon the Grid Engine scheduler, which leverages public testbeds as test environments. We present empirical findings derived from these deployments. The paper demonstrates that integrating fault tolerance into HPC environments is a complex endeavor, with Grid and compute nodes exhibiting distinct fault-tolerant characteristics. Grids, distinguished by their heterogeneous architecture, are particularly vulnerable to faults. This study introduces a novel fault-tolerant HPC system named FTGrid, designed to operate within public testbeds. FTGrid integrates and extends established fault-tolerant models, specifically VFT and Cosmos, while offering a user-friendly interface. To validate FTGrid's effectiveness, we evaluated its performance across public testbeds located in India and the EU. Our results indicate that significant efforts are still needed to ensure fault tolerance in public testbeds and grids, reinforcing the necessity of rigorous empirical evaluation. Additionally, we examined the specific nuances of Grid and compute node failures, offering a practical perspective on their reliability.

By employing a robust set of statistically independent predictions from the simplest inflationary scenarios, we aim to identify the region of cosmological parameter space compatible with a $\Lambda$CDM framework featuring a single type of cold dark matter. Our results indicate that while single-field inflationary models successfully predict the observed two-point correlation function of density fluctuations, they struggle to account for the four-point correlation function. Specifically, within the single-field context, excluding multi-component dark matter, the crossover scale—where correlations transition from positive to negative—shifts to significantly smaller values than observed. This discrepancy suggests that either the simplest inflationary models or the cold dark matter hypothesis is incorrect. We note, however, that if warm dark matter is considered, the crossover scale moves toward larger values, aligning with observations. Consequently, the simplest cold dark matter models appear to be ruled out, a conclusion that remains robust even when accounting for non-Gaussianities generated during inflation. This finding reinforces the hypothesis of warm dark matter and underscores the need for more intricate and testable inflationary models. Finally, we discuss the implications of these findings for current and future cosmological surveys. These models remain testable through upcoming measurements of the angular power spectrum of the cosmic microwave background and the large-scale structure of the universe, as well as the amplitude of small-scale density fluctuations. Additionally, the paper examines the potential of utilizing the bispectrum of density fluctuations to constrain inflationary models. We demonstrate that complete consistency preservation—where a theory's complete extensions share the same continuous minimal model—holds precisely when the original theory does, in the context of cont-min. Furthermore, we adapt the Loś-Tarski Theorem and continuous Loś's Theorem to continuous first-order logic with min, thereby establishing an equivalent characterization of complete consistency preservation for such theories. Finally, we apply these findings to min-max continuous logic, noting that while min-max is not a partial ordering, transforming any such theory into an equivalent one where min and max are separated yields a result where min satisfies the conditions for our equivalent characterization of complete consistency preservation. Our work also extends to soft minimum continuous logic, a setting where min is replaced by a parameterized "soft min" function. This generalization is particularly relevant for von Neumann-Minkowski geometry, as the set of metric spaces constitutes the continuous minimal model of a specific theory where the soft min function corresponds to the Yau-Tsiang minimum. In this context, our equivalent formulation of the Loś-Tarski Theorem offers a novel, purely logical method for characterizing the complete theories of finite-dimensional Yau-Tsiang spaces. Additionally, we examine the relationship between min and soft min, showing that the parameterization of soft min can be defined using only min, max, addition, and multiplication. Consequently, soft min cannot be ignored in a theory simply because it appears unnecessary at first glance, as it is entirely determined by these other operations. This has significant implications for the study of finite-dimensional metric spaces.

The $h$-number of this set, denoted $h(a_1, \dots, a_n)$, represents the count of irreducible expressions of the form $ax - h(R(ax))$, where $x$ is an integer, $h(R(ax)) < 2ax$, and the expression is irreducible if no positive integers $x, y$ satisfy $ax = \sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i$ with $0 < x_i \leq h(a_1, \dots, a_n)$ for all $i$. The largest integer that cannot be expressed in this form is known as the Frobenius number, denoted $F(a_1, \dots, a_n)$. This paper introduces an algorithm to calculate the $h$-number and a formula to determine the Frobenius number using the $h$-number. Additionally, a conjecture regarding the upper bound of the Frobenius number is proposed. The algorithm and formula presented here enable the verification of the Nakamura-Kohno-Ishikawa conjecture for any set of at least two positive integers. This work introduces a new, compact equation of state for finite temperature QCD, designed for numerical relativity simulations, which integrates perturbative QCD, the Monte Carlo generated Hadron Resonance Gas, and quark-diquark perturbative quantum chromodynamics. When extrapolated to zero temperature, this novel hadron Resonance Gas component aligns with the Model Independent Taurino Baym-Mottl framework at low temperatures and transitions into a high-temperature perturbative QCD description at the quark-hadron transition, effectively serving as a hadronic version of the Mottl-Musoltz-Perturbative QCD (MPQ) model. This study examines how developers select among three distinct channels—collocated speech, remote chat, and remote collaboration—based on their intended goals. Through two sequential experiments, we first presented developers with pairs of goals and asked them to select their preferred channel, thereby identifying goal-based channel selection patterns. Second, by logging actual remote interactions, we identified properties that distinguish speech from chat. The findings indicate that when knowledge transfer is the goal, developers predominantly choose remote collaborative editing, yet they also frequently select chat. Conversely, when coordinating work is the goal, developers overwhelmingly prefer remote collaborative editing. Distinctive features of recorded remote chat sessions include a high volume of questions, a preponderance of declarative statements, and a low count of imperative sentences. These results offer a deeper understanding of how remote collaborative editing, chat, and speech complement one another, serving as a foundation for smarter virtual communication assistants. Specifically, virtual agents can leverage these insights to proactively suggest alternative communication channels.

Remote pair programming sessions often suffer from reduced productivity and communication breakdowns, primarily because developers struggle to choose the most suitable communication channel. To address this, we introduce a system called VACC (a Virtual Agent that Chooses Communication Channels), designed to detect remote collaboration activities and suggest appropriate communication mediums. Built upon a classification model that distinguishes between remote collaborative editing and chat, VACC analyzes a developer's current communication to predict whether transferring knowledge or coordinating work is required, subsequently recommending the optimal channel. An empirical study involving 12 developers confirmed that human annotators can reliably differentiate between remote collaborative editing and chat with high accuracy. Our results demonstrate that VACC successfully prompts remote collaborators to switch to more appropriate communication channels, thereby fostering a greater awareness of communication choices and improving the efficiency of remote collaborative software development.

In remote collaborative software development, selecting the appropriate communication channel is crucial for conveying information effectively. However, humans often default to a single channel, such as chat, regardless of context, which can hinder communication. This paper presents an automated solution to dynamically select the optimal channel during virtual pair programming. Our approach, supported by virtual agents, analyzes remote collaborative activities to determine the necessary information and suggest the most suitable communication channel. This decision-making process is derived from a Goal-Question-Meta model (GQM) tailored to the remote collaborative software development domain. We implemented a proof-of-concept system to validate our approach, developing an algorithm capable of distinguishing between remote collaborative editing and chat

This paper introduces a novel machine learning model designed to automatically extract features from URL encodings and content to classify legitimate versus malicious links. We demonstrate that these two factors can be distinguished by analyzing the evolution of the stellar mass-to-light ratio ($\epsilon$) across different wavelengths. Specifically, if early Universe conditions are the primary driver, $\epsilon$ should remain relatively stable over time. Conversely, if the physics of star formation plays a significant role, $\epsilon$ is expected to decrease as galaxies age. The method is particularly effective for detecting abrupt changes, including those caused by malicious attacks, and is especially relevant for large-scale systems like computer networks where the underlying dynamics are well-modeled by low-rank transition matrices. We develop a statistical test to identify these occurrences and demonstrate that it enjoys strong theoretical guarantees, specifically exponential error bounds, provided the process is not perfectly deterministic. Furthermore, we evaluate the method through numerical experiments and successfully apply it to a real-world cyber-physical system: a network of web servers.

The core mechanism of our approach involves monitoring the evolution of the Markov chain's distribution. Since the chain is defined by a transition matrix with a known, fixed rank, we can leverage this low-rank property to create a compact representation of the distribution. An anomaly is flagged when the transition matrix responsible for the observed distribution evolution deviates significantly from the nominal (expected) matrix. This detection framework is particularly powerful because it remains robust against noise and can identify changes even when the support of the distribution shifts.

We establish statistical bounds for a test that measures the distance between two sets of observations, each generated by a different Markov chain. These bounds highlight the exponential rate at which detection errors decrease as the number of observations increases. Our analysis shows that this result holds as long as each Markov chain is not purely deterministic, meaning it possesses a minimum level of randomness.

In the experimental section, we present our algorithm alongside a baseline approach, comparing their performance in terms of detection accuracy and computational cost. We tested both methods in two scenarios: first, using synthetic data to verify our theoretical findings; and second, by applying the algorithm to a real-world network of web servers to assess its practical viability. These experiments confirm that our proposed method outperforms the baseline, offering a compelling alternative for anomaly detection in discrete-time Markov chains.

To investigate whether these groups form a single chain or consist of independent clusters, we analyzed proper motions and kinematics of nearby stars using a machine learning approach. We identified a YSO group located at an angular distance of roughly 1.5 degrees from the primary cluster, sharing similar proper motions and a distance modulus of 13.5 ± 0.5. These findings suggest the presence of a linear chain of young stellar groups spanning a total length of 4.5 kpc. This is the first reported discovery of such a chain in the Galactic disk, and its characteristics may offer insights into the formation of long filamentary structures in other galaxies. Additionally, we identified a YSO group at 0.75 degrees from the main cluster with a distance modulus of 14.5 ± 0.5, indicating it lies at an intermediate distance between the primary cluster and the farthest group. We conclude that these distant YSO groups are likely not associated with the main cluster, as they lack evidence of being part of a larger, more distant cluster. These distant groups may serve as valuable tracers for studying the structure of the Galactic disk. Finally, we propose that the most distant YSO group could be a member of the Perseus Arm. The discovery of these chains highlights the utility of applying machine learning techniques to Galactic structure research. Our findings suggest that similar stellar chains may exist in other galaxies, a topic for future exploration. This paper examines the consistency of such proposals by applying the Swampland Distance Conjecture to a black hole within a massive tower. This application reveals a tension: the finiteness of black hole entropy appears to conflict with the expected behavior of the tower's mass gap. This contradiction suggests that naive extensions of the Swampland program are flawed and implies that proposals aiming to reconstruct swamulands from observed black hole physics must incorporate additional mechanisms, such as stringy fuzz or quantum gravity effects. These necessities align with current efforts to recover swamuland data from black hole entropy. Furthermore, we offer a heuristic derivation of the Distance Conjecture from the first law of surface gravity, which also yields a finite correction term corresponding to the tower mass. This finding supports the view that stringy fuzz or similar structures are essential. Finally, we note that similar contradictions arise when applying other Swamuland conjectures. These results reinforce the idea that any successful program for reconstructing swamuland physics must account for the expected corrections to the horizon's nature. This requirement is consistent with recent advances in the gravity dual of a black hole's near-horizon region. Additionally, we provide a review of the holographic construction of the Swamuland Landscape. Together, these points indicate that significant progress has been made toward realizing the dream of deducing stringy physics from black hole observations. This dream is now grounded in concrete theoretical achievements. Furthermore, we outline the specific questions and challenges that must be addressed to achieve the ultimate goal of fully reconstructing swamuland data. This framework provides motivation and direction for subsequent research. The system comprises a stack of glass-epoxy plates, each containing a metallic patch. When an external MW electric field is applied, it induces an oscillating current along the patch's length. In a single-layer configuration, this oscillation manifests as a transverse voltage across the patch. By connecting this transverse voltage in series between adjacent plates, the system achieves a cumulative response that scales with the number of layers. This approach maintains a compact footprint, as the antenna dimensions remain unchanged regardless of how many layers are added. Experimental validation demonstrates that this method yields a $40$ dB gain in signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) and a fourfold increase in detection sensitivity compared to a standard single-layer antenna. These findings confirm that a multi-layer design can effectively sense weak signals as low as $\mu$V/m. Furthermore, the methodology is highly scalable, allowing for additional sensitivity improvements by simply increasing the number of layers. Beyond its application in sensing, this dielectric antenna platform offers a versatile framework for investigating various physical phenomena, including near-field to far-field transitions, antenna re-radiation characteristics, and the impact of environmental factors on detection performance. Additionally, the technique supports dielectric integration, enabling the deployment of large-area sensors within a single experimental setup. Ultimately, this innovative antenna design presents a significant advancement over conventional metallic antennas, which often suffer from complex manufacturing and limited scalability. As a proof of concept, the multi-layer antenna was successfully employed to detect the fundamental radiation from an electronic oscillator and the near-field of a mobile phone. These results establish a new, simple, and scalable strategy for creating advanced MW electric field antennas with enhanced performance. Furthermore, the methodology holds potential for diverse applications, such as developing wearable sensing systems. This research was conducted under the EU-funded WISE project. While a conventional model accounting for a bulge, disk, and halo predicts a rotation curve that rises and then declines, observations show a nearly flat rotation curve extending to a maximum radius of approximately 15 kpc. This mismatch implies an unaccounted mass of roughly $10^{10} M_{\odot}$ within the inner 15 kpc. Potential sources for this excess mass include a massive central bar, a massive bulge, or a massive central molecular disk. However, the absence of a prominent H$\alpha$ bulge and HST imaging data indicate that a massive bulge is unlikely. Our findings reveal that the bulge is indeed negligible, but the central disk is not only massive but also dynamically "hotter" than the surrounding regions. These results suggest that the central disk is dynamically decoupled from the inner gas and stellar components. Furthermore, we demonstrate that a self-gravitating disk can account for the observed rotation curve. This study represents the first detection of a massive, self-gravitating disk in a spiral galaxy. This event prompted the development of a beam monitoring system to detect and localize proton beams within the machine's tunnel and underground areas. These detectors are now fully installed in the LHC vicinity, and their results demonstrate that the BLM system has maintained high availability throughout the accelerator's operation. Furthermore, the BLM system has proven to be an invaluable research and development tool for the LHC experiments.

Due to the inherent sparsity of real-world data, existing reasoning methods for KG completion struggle to generalize to unseen subject-object or predicate pairs. The generator constructs various reasoning paths grounded in the knowledge graph schema, which subsequently guide the completer to predict missing entities or predicates. Extensive experiments across multiple benchmark knowledge graphs demonstrate that RRR significantly outperforms prior state-of-the-art methods. Additionally, rrr-gpt-3.5-turbo achieves performance comparable to rrr-gpt-3.5-turbo while reducing training costs by three orders of magnitude. Graph classification is a critical task in graph machine learning with significant real-world applications. However, a key limitation of many existing approaches is their reliance on fully labeled datasets, a requirement that is often impractical to meet. To address this, we propose a new active learning approach for clustering a large set of unlabeled graphs. This method utilizes a semi-supervised graph contrastive learning model to generate graph representations, which are then used to build a classifier that predicts graph classes. This classifier identifies geometrically diverse unlabeled groups to serve as anchors, guiding the contrastive learning process. Furthermore, we develop a clustering algorithm based on these geometric representations to group similar unlabeled graphs. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets reveal that our method significantly improves geometric representation learning compared to supervised and unsupervised baselines. Moreover, our approach achieves superior performance in both geometric diversity and clustering accuracy relative to state-of-the-art methods. Our code can be accessed at https://github.com/soheilsalehi/GCLCL.

This study introduces a novel method for reversing partisan bias caused by districting, operating without assuming a specific districting algorithm. We formulate this problem as a linear program that minimizes reversible votes, requiring only pre- and post-census population counts and historical election results. Our linear programming approach successfully reverses bias in various real-world elections with minimal impact on voter numbers. Furthermore, we demonstrate that reversing bias without significantly altering outcomes is often impossible when districts are drawn using chaotic methods, such as those employed in Arizona. Additionally, we explore a variant that alters partisan balance only in districts currently experiencing split-ticket voting, presenting a linear programming formulation that achieves this with the minimum necessary alterations. Numerical experiments on real elections indicate that this modified method typically requires fewer changes than fully reversing bias. We also provide a "reverse engineering" application: given historical election data and approximate reversal costs, we can infer the districting algorithm most likely responsible, offering a straightforward minimum-distance approach to this challenge. Finally, we propose a policy-driven method for reversing bias that generates a set of alternative districting plans, each eliminating bias in at least one election. This approach utilizes a multi-objective optimization framework incorporating equity and compactness criteria, with an algorithm designed to produce a diverse collection of solutions. Although this method alters more votes than others, it ensures that every district achieves a partisan balance of zero. We conclude with a discussion of the inherent trade-offs among these various approaches to undistricting. Across all scenarios, reversing bias is achievable with minimal alterations to historical election data, yet no method can eliminate all forms of distortion. Consequently, legislators must carefully evaluate the distinct advantages and limitations of each undistricting strategy. Ultimately, legislative action is required to establish a framework for creating fair districting plans; merely reversing existing plans does not constitute a complete solution.
