To address this, we introduce the Free-Body Ellipsoid (FBE), a novel, computationally efficient ellipsoid type designed for applications involving multiple bodies and manipulators. An FBE models a body as a free object influenced by various manipulators, with its orientation and size determined by the combined effects of these manipulators. security of a broad spectrum of cryptographic protocols, encompassing both secure computation and communication. We consider protocols involving multiple parties, each holding private inputs and executing their designated steps without trusting others to execute theirs. The model operates under two core assumptions: (1) parties possess no prior shared information, and (2) an adversary controls the network, deciding which messages are delivered, lost, or intercepted. To represent our protocol and communication network structures, we utilize graph theory. Specifically, we define a protocol graph where vertices represent parties and edges denote directed trust relationships; similarly, a communication network graph has vertices for parties and edges for direct network connections. Assuming these protocol and network graphs are known to the adversary, we examine the most fundamental security question: under what conditions can the adversary, by manipulating message delivery, force a party to output incorrect results? By leveraging graph-theoretic properties of the adversary graph relative to the network graph, we derive a precise condition guaranteeing correct output even against a fully malicious adversary. We also present a straightforward algorithm for verifying this condition and discuss potential extensions. Finally, we apply this framework to several secure computation and communication scenarios to identify the necessary assumptions on protocol and network graph structures that ensure correct computation. This approach allows for the design of secure protocols that function correctly even when individual network links fail. Keywords: Graph Theory, Security.

Although model compression techniques have been extensively researched, current methods often fail to achieve a balanced trade-off among accuracy, resource usage, and processing speed. This paper introduces a novel DCNN compression approach that leverages the predictive capabilities of DCNN layers. Specifically, we propose using the output of one layer to forecast the activations of a subsequent skip target layer. To minimize the error between predicted and actual target activations, we incorporate this mechanism into the training of the skip target layer. This dynamic feedback loop, where layers anticipate each other's states, creates mutual dependencies that strengthen the connection between interacting layers. Empirical results demonstrate that the inter-layer connections established by our method contain critical information, enabling the removal of redundant data. Consequently, we achieve significant model size reduction and computational savings with only a marginal impact on accuracy. We have validated the efficacy and universality of this approach across various models and tasks, including image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation. Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) for speech recognition by leveraging the specific characteristics of speech. We demonstrate that DNN layers processing speech exhibits a natural redundancy, allowing for the reduction of redundant information without significantly compromising recognition accuracy. Two approaches are presented to exploit this redundancy: (i) a new architecture, the Factorized Hierarchical Deep Boltzmann Machine (FHDBM), which utilizes shared deterministic factors to capture redundancy across multiple levels of a DNN, and (ii) U-Net style architectures, which employ deterministic bottleneck factors to encode redundant details within speech. Both methods yield DNNs with improved computational efficiency and higher accuracy. Specifically, the U-Net based DNN achieves a 41% reduction in forward computation cost while maintaining equivalent recognition accuracy compared to a standard DNN. Furthermore, the proposed architectures effectively model the temporal structure inherent in speech, resulting in better accuracy than a regular DNN of equivalent size. Experimental results confirm the significant potential of these proposed DNNs for practical applications.

It examines the data obtained from these sensitive searches to establish constraints on model-independent scattering cross sections, thereby outlining significant limitations for nearly all subclasses of massive particle dark matter. Consequently, this work defines the highly sensitive "discovery threshold" necessary for these experiments to successfully identify dark matter. Furthermore, the discussion explores how to leverage this threshold to investigate alternative scenarios, including sub-GeV fermionic dark matter, massive bosonic dark matter with measurable lifetimes, and the potential for detecting entire classes of particle dark matter through non-resonant production mechanisms. Finally, we address the impending era of data abundance, driven by the rapid accumulation of information from increasingly sensitive experiments, and emphasize the critical role of interpreting this future data within a broad theoretical framework. This approach ensures that the extraordinary sensitivity achieved by direct detection is fully utilized to constrain all substantial classes of massive particle dark matter. Sufficiently sensitive direct detection experiments will either discover dark matter or establish a comprehensive set of limits that exclude its existence as a massive particle. In this context, we also highlight the necessity of developing new detection mechanisms to achieve the same level of completeness when searching for interactions with specific massive particle dark matter candidates. These objectives will be met by the next generation of large-scale, high-precision experiments, which are currently in the planning and early construction phases. These initiatives aim to establish direct detection as a discovery engine for massive particle dark matter, capable of achieving a signal-to-background ratio of 1:1, alongside direct and indirect detection methods. Collectively, these efforts will enable the complete discovery or rigorous exclusion of all substantial classes of massive particle dark matter. This represents a historic turning point in the field, marking the discovery threshold for massive particle dark matter via direct detection. Following this, we explore the era of "post-massive particle dark matter," where direct detection will shift its focus to the most subtle forms of non-massive particle dark matter, such as virtual dark matter and dark photons. This research demonstrates that direct detection will not only discover massive particle dark matter but will also uncover the physical nature of all substantial classes of particle dark matter. This represents a new discovery threshold for direct detection, representing the ultimate sensitivity limit of the technique. The realization of this goal will be driven by the forthcoming multi-messenger program, which will integrate data from direct and indirect detection with insights from collider experiments and astrophysical observations. Collectively, these initiatives will establish the fundamental laws of particle dark matter. This represents a second historic discovery

While model pruning offers a path to creating lightweight ASR systems, it often degrades performance by treating network weights as deterministic values. In contrast, weight quantization can maintain high accuracy while significantly reducing model size by acknowledging the stochastic nature of low-precision weights. This paper introduces a systematic framework for jointly optimizing neural network architecture and the bit-widths of quantized weights in ASR models. By employing a differentiable search method, we automatically determine optimal architectures and weight bit-widths, enabling the creation of efficient, end-to-end ASR neural architectures. Our approach, which supports both additive and convolutional networks, was evaluated on the Switchboard ASR task using an additive attention-based model. The resulting pruned and quantized ASR model achieves an A-word error rate of 24.1%, outperforming a pruned unquantized model by 1.4%. Furthermore, our method generates diverse, tailored architectures and individual weight bit-widths for each layer, surpassing the uniform low-bit-width pruning of previous studies. Finally, we demonstrate the scalability of our approach by applying it to a larger ASR task.

Consequently, this approach enables a conceptual grasp of the abstract architecture of modal logic. Furthermore, by leveraging the machinery of topological categories, we can derive key results in modal logic, such as the completeness of the S5 logic relative to its standard semantic approach. Most significantly, this perspective illuminates the connections between fundamental structural properties of topological categories and important logical concepts, thereby providing a foundational understanding of major completeness theorems in modal logic.

As IoT devices proliferate, security threats to neural network infrastructure are escalating, necessitating robust and adaptable security mechanisms. This article introduces a security framework for neural networks within IoT environments, integrating a Blockchain-based security layer with a Deep Learning (DL) model. The proposed solution leverages Blockchain's security attributes and smart contracts to fortify DL models, ensuring the integrity of trained weights and their application during prediction. Additionally, Blockchain facilitates secure, privacy-preserving DL model training through federated learning by verifying the authenticity of local models contributed by IoT devices via smart contracts. To support these operations, the framework employs a DL-enhanced Blockchain network that dynamically adjusts gas fees based on the computational capacity of contributing devices, optimizing gas usage during training and prediction phases. Furthermore, the system utilizes a specific Blockchain network for this purpose and gas fee prediction. The approach has been implemented and evaluated using public datasets, with results demonstrating that the proposed solution effectively secures DL models within Blockchain networks. The implementation code is accessible at: https://github.com/abhishekgupta1234567890/IoT-Blockchain-Deep-Learning. The paper is structured as follows: Section II reviews related work; Section III details the proposed solution; Section IV presents the results of performance evaluations; and Section V concludes the study.

Leveraging the concept of linear relative error, this study adapts two first-order optimization methods—Rosen's Rosenbrock method and the Broyden-Frommer method—for use in policy iteration. These approaches, termed Rosenbrock policy iteration and relative Broyden-policy iteration, lower the local convergence complexity to linear. We establish that both methods are suitable for regular MDPs, defined as those containing a core policy whose value function acts as a contraction under the maximum absolute difference operator. Furthermore, when applied to regular continuous MDPs featuring Lipschitz-continuous transition probability operators, the Rosenbrock policy iteration achieves local asymptotic convergence with an order-2 convergent operator, whereas relative Broyden-policy iteration yields an order-1 convergent operator. Numerical experiments demonstrate that both proposed algorithms outperform standard policy iteration in computational efficiency. Notably, the relative Broyden-policy iteration is particularly effective for irregular continuous MDPs, a scenario where relative Rosenbrock policy iteration and other polynomial methods fail to converge. The relative Broyden-policy iteration is implemented in the Python-based PyMBDP package and is accessible for download. This work was developed during the second author's internship at the first author's institution.

This paper introduces R, a straightforward random variable generator designed for use within Rel, a relativistic particle simulator written in C. R supports both uniform and Gaussian distributions and integrates seamlessly with Rel, which currently handles relativistic electron beam propagation through space-charge-dominated magnetic and electrostatic fields. The combined R+Rel system is presented as a potential tool for modeling both stochastic and deterministic aspects of particle accelerators and experimental facilities. To demonstrate its utility, the paper applies this approach to two scenarios: first, analyzing how initial energy spread affects the emittance growth of a proton micro-bunch traversing a periodic array of drifts and decelerators; second, exploring how the R+Rel tool can assist accelerator experiment planners in estimating the statistical significance of data obtained when the initial energy spread of the test protons is unknown. In this context, 'R' symbolizes the random variables inherent in experimental measurements, whereas 'rel' denotes the relative uncertainty in those measurements. Source code for R and Rel, along with a user guide, sample input files, and output examples, are available at: http://www.ipp.mpg.de/~fisch/rplusrel/.

In this work, we further examine the relationship between different Ricci curvature notions in Finsler spaces by exploring various angle conditions. Specifically, we define two additional Ricci curvatures, $ \curvmap_1 $ and $ \curvmap_2 $, through "left" and "right" angle conditions, respectively. We then analyze the interconnections among $ \curvmap $, $ \curvmap_1 $, and $ \curvmap_2 $ within the context of Finsler spaces that have nonnegative flag curvature. Our findings reveal that for Finsler spaces with nonnegative flag curvature, the recently proposed "Busemann-Hausdorff Ricci curvature" ( $ \curvmap $ ) and the "Bergman Ricci curvature" ( $ \curvmap_2 $ ) coincide if and only if the space exhibits Berwald curvature. Finally, we demonstrate that a Finsler space characterized by nonnegative flag curvature and satisfying $ \curvmap \ge 0 $ satisfies the convexity condition if and only if it possesses nonnegative Ricci curvature. This result offers a novel approach to reestablishing Liouville theorems for Finsler manifolds with nonnegative Ricci curvature and compact indicatrices.

This paper aims to establish identities involving basic hypergeometric series that correspond to these Apéry-type binomial series. By utilizing these identities, we derive numerous new equations featuring products of factorials and binomial coefficients, as well as reciprocal sums of such products. Additionally, several infinite series containing q-analogs of factorials and binomial coefficients emerge as natural q-analogs of the original Apéry-type binomial series identities. These findings lead to identities involving basic hypergeometric series and provide a method for evaluating special values of special functions, such as the Riemann zeta function, the digamma function, and the polygamma function. Furthermore, we present specific examples of q-analogs of Apéry-type binomial series that yield identities with the q-Digamma function, the q-Riemann zeta function, special values of the Riemann polylogarithm, special values of the Hurwitz zeta function, and special values of the derivative of the Dedekind eta function. Finally, we conjecture an identity for the q-analog of the Apéry-type binomial series that is equivalent to a relation involving the derivative of the Dedekind eta function and its reciprocal. Apéry's original identities are recovered as limiting cases when $q \to 1$. Keywords: Apéry-type binomial series, basic hypergeometric series, q-Digamma function, derivative of the Dedekind eta function, polygamma function, Hurwitz zeta function, and the equivalent of the Riemann zeta function. 3126.89-104426.1 (WISEA), a candidate young stellar object (YSO) located in the Galactic plane, revealed a point source exhibiting a periodic light curve with a period of 1.601 ± 0.001 days. This object was initially identified as a potential eclipsing binary in a 2019 study by Li et al. However, a reanalysis of the same photometric data, incorporating light from an adjacent star, indicates that the observed periodicity actually stems from the accretion variability of a nearby companion. We conducted near-infrared spectroscopy of WISEA J133126.89-104426.1 using the Keck/MOSFIRE instrument, characterizing it as a K5-M0 binary with an 11:5 flux ratio in the J band. The primary component displays strong Hα emission, while the secondary component shows no detectable emission lines. Additionally, we performed near-infrared spectroscopy on the second variable star, identified as WISEA J153126.89-104426.1 (the same object previously analyzed by Li et al. 2019), which exhibits a significantly bluer spectral energy distribution than the source mentioned in the title. Our findings suggest that the object designated WISEA J133126.89-104426.1 is a young stellar object with a spectral type of K5-M0, possessing a mass of approximately 0.7 solar masses and an age of roughly 10 million years. Its variability is driven by accretion processes, with a best-fit accretion rate of log(M/Ṁ*) = -3.5. The previously reported 1.6-day period likely results from aliasing in the sampling of the light curve. The second object, wISEA J153126.89-104426.1, is a low-mass YSO with a mass of approximately 0.2 solar masses and an age of about 10 million years. Its variability is also attributed to accretion, with a best-fit rate of log(Ṁ*/Ṁ*) = -4.5. Both objects are situated within the Upper Scorpius OB association, a known star-forming region. The test samples were prepared in two forms: one containing only fine grains, and another with an equivalent volume of fine grains mixed in-situ with larger grains matching typical surface conditions on both Mars and the Moon. The applied confining pressure served as a model for the expected Martian atmospheric pressure. Key findings indicate that the fine-grained regolith exhibits higher strength than its Lunar counterpart, a discrepancy that grows as the Martian confining pressure increases. Furthermore, the Martian simulant demonstrates greater ductility and a lower friction angle compared to the Lunar simulant. The peak strength of both materials was found to be approximately 20% greater under a Martian-like confining pressure of 0.7 kPa compared to vacuum or 101.3 kPa (1 atm) Earth-like conditions. These results have significant implications for the design of In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU) systems on both celestial bodies. Specifically, the data suggests that the Martian confining pressure substantially enhances the load-bearing capacity of Martian regolith. Consequently, engineering designs for Mars should capitalize on this increased capacity, potentially offering a relative advantage over Lunar structures due to the planet's atmosphere. Conversely, this pressure-induced strength increase may pose challenges for certain excavation operations on Mars. Ultimately, these findings underscore the critical role of grain-size distribution in the mechanical behavior of regolith simulant and real lunar and Martian regolith. This grain-size effect is more pronounced in Martian confining pressure than in vacuum or Earth-like atmospheric conditions. The study concludes that the grain-size influence is most evident when the Martian confining pressure is 0.7 kPa. Additionally, a power-law function was developed to quantify the effect of confining pressure on the mechanical properties of both Lunar and Martian regolith simulants. Finally, the report proposes a new classification system for Martian and Lunar regolith mechanical properties, which can be utilized to select appropriate formulas for calculating the pressure required for in-situ greenhouse construction using ISRU techniques. Keywords: ISRU, Martian regolith, Lunar regolith, confining pressure, grain-size distribution, mechanical properties, Martian atmosphere, greenhouses. (2021). Tensors $G_2$ is explicitly provided for each of the eight classified toric $G_2$-surfaces, which correspond to eight distinct toric divisors. The study also identifies and examines the complex elliptic surfaces associated with these toric $G_2$-manifolds. Together, these results expand the known list of four-dimensional toric $G_2$-manifolds from eight to fourteen. Furthermore, this work connects with other recent studies on tensors by demonstrating that all twelve toric Fano fourfolds previously identified as possessing non-flat torsion tensors now fall into one of two categories: either they represent new torsion types, or they are established as toric $G_2$-manifolds (as detailed in this paper). Additionally, the paper introduces a method for determining the torsion of an elliptic surface derived from a toric $G_2$-manifold through a "reverse" procedure. By combining findings from this paper and that method, we can conclude that any elliptic surface featuring a specific list of singular fibers can be realized as a toric $G_2$-manifold with a well-defined upper limit on its torsion. In the forthcoming Part II, we will establish an algorithm to construct the corresponding toric $G_2$-manifold and reduce its torsion to zero. Specifically, we will demonstrate that the tensors associated with toric $G_2$-manifolds can be eliminated by performing blow-ups along toric divisors linked to specific toric curves. Furthermore, we will provide a classification of the resulting toric $G_2$-manifolds with vanishing torsion, thereby completing the program of classifying all four-dimensional toric $G_2$-manifolds. Finally, we will establish an upper bound on the number of distinct toric $G_2$-manifolds when categorized by their smooth projective toric orbit spaces.

usion model describing how a new species invades a territory by replacing an existing one, is examined here through the lens of delayed reactions. The approach involves training a statistical model that maps phoneme sequence features to phoneme-acoustic transition features, where the latter are derived from counting the occurrences of specific phoneme transitions within an acoustic database. Acoustic predictions are generated using a feed-forward neural network, which is trained via backpropagation through the phoneme sequence features. Experimental results demonstrate that this neural network-based acoustical duration modeling achieves a mean absolute error of 20.2 ms, outperforming Weiphong et al.'s tone-based RBF method, which recorded an error of 26.4 ms. Furthermore, when integrated with Weiphong et al.'s tone prediction algorithm, this proposed method yields natural-sounding synthetic speech. Additionally, the approach offers a significant advantage by eliminating the need for separate tone prediction training on specific speaker groups, thereby greatly enhancing its scalability. The effectiveness of this neural acoustical duration modeling was validated using both natural and synthetic voice group acoustic databases. To ensure the method's applicability, a new tone normalization technique was also proposed. Finally, the approach was implemented within a neural speech synthesis system, yielding promising results. Occupancy models serve as a fundamental tool for analyzing species distribution data, offering the benefit of simultaneously estimating detection and occurrence probabilities. However, numerous model assumptions have been identified as sources of bias, with prior work predominantly highlighting the risks of spatial heterogeneity in occurrence probabilities. In this work, we investigate the impact of heterogeneity in detection probabilities, a topic receiving less attention. We develop an occupancy model allowing detection probabilities to vary by distance from the center of the survey area, estimating parameters for central, edge, and perimeter distances. Our findings reveal that a common shortcut—assuming constant detection probability while letting occupancy rates vary spatially—results in overestimated occupancy rates when detection probability actually varies by distance from the center. Additionally, we show that the distance-dependent detection probability model can misidentify a species as absent at distant sites if detection probability is truly constant, simply because the species was never detected there. Finally, we offer practical guidance for applying this model to real data.

This framework treats data points as realizations of a latent variable model governed by a joint probability density function (PDF), which is approximated using a Gaussian copula composed of univariate marginal distributions. Each distribution's mean and variance are treated as learnable parameters. By applying a combination of variational inference and maximum likelihood estimation, the model is optimized to ensure the marginal likelihood of the data remains high. During training, the model is exposed to a random sample from a standard Gaussian distribution; consequently, after convergence, the standard Gaussian latent variable's marginal likelihood approximates that of the observed data. This approach enables the PAE to simultaneously learn a mapping from data to latent variables and the underlying joint distribution, offering an alternative to traditional autoencoders. Unlike standard autoencoders, the PAE explicitly models dependencies between latent variables through their multivariate distribution. Furthermore, the probabilistic nature of the model allows for the quantification of uncertainty in the learned mapping and distribution. To demonstrate the PAE's ability to capture physically-relevant latent variables, we apply it to a dataset of two-dimensional incompressible fluid flows characterized by the periodic forcing of a square obstacle. In this scenario, the latent variables are identified as the obstacle's center position $(x_c, y_c)$, with the forcing period $T$ defining the timescale for the variables to transition between positions. Using data from 256 equidistant time steps spanning 200 periods, models trained with varying hyperparameters successfully encode the obstacle's position and density within a 200 by 200 by $N$-dimensional space (where $N=20$ for a specific configuration). Finally, we assess the PAE's uncertainty quantification capabilities by comparing the uncertainty in the latent variable mapping against the uncertainty in the approximate joint PDF at specific data points. These results indicate that the PAE effectively captures the obstacle's position, maintains a low reconstruction error, and reliably quantifies uncertainty. This MRAM device operates by utilizing the spin polarization inherent in these materials to switch bits via torque. We introduce a concept for achieving such a device using a spin-polarized ferromagnetic (FM) gate that modulates the tunneling current through a nonmagnetic (NM) buffer layer via the magneto-optical Kerr effect. By employing a circularly polarized probe laser diode within an optical readout setup, we can detect the FM's magnetization direction by measuring variations in tunneling resistance. The selected NM buffer layers, such as CrIX$_3$, are tunable, offering potential for circular Kerr effect detection at room temperature. This study investigates the evolution of magnetic field configurations and differential rotation in these stars, specifically examining how fields aligned with the rotation axis or the equator are influenced by changes in rotation profiles as the stars age. Our three-dimensional, non-ideal magnetohydrodynamic simulations reveal that magnetic helicity and magnetic energy fluctuate periodically during the main-sequence phase due to the evolution of differential rotation, whereas they increase continuously during the pre-main-sequence and post-main-sequence stages. In recent years, deepfake technology has advanced rapidly, enabling the creation of highly realistic fake videos that pose significant challenges for detection. While numerous detection methods have emerged, they often struggle with the domain shift caused by variations in generation tools, leading to inconsistent performance. To date, no comprehensive benchmark exists for evaluating deepfake detection, creating a barrier to effectively comparing and replicating results across different algorithms. To overcome this, we introduce DeepFaceDB, a large-scale, diverse, and systematic deepfake database designed to facilitate the evaluation of deepface detection across different techniques. This repository is available at https://github.com/DeepFaceDB. Additionally, we propose a novel detection framework, DeepFaceDetector, which demonstrates superior performance on existing benchmarks compared to state-of-the-art methods. We have also released the code for this detector at https://github.com/yzhang1210/DeepFaceDetector. Our contributions include: (1) the introduction of DeepFaceDB, a rigorous and diverse database for assessing deepface detection methods; (2) the proposal of DeepFaceDetector, a new detector that achieves state-of-the-art performance; and (3) the release of source codes for both DeepFaceDetector and DeepFaceDB to foster future research. The proposed methods achieve state-of-the-art results on the O-Face and CAS-FFS datasets. The deepfake detector can identify over 99% of malicious deepfake accounts on WhatsApp within 20 minutes, offering a practical and efficient solution. We believe these contributions will inspire further research in detecting and mitigating deepfake threats. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/yzhang1210/DeepFaceDetector and the database at https://github.com/yzhang1210/DeepFaceDB.

Under the assumption of exchangeability, we derive an explicit formula for the probability that $n$ individuals, observed at specific random times, share the same age-ancestry tree. This formula relies on the Palm-2-measure, which describes the statistical distribution of the process when a point is selected at random. Furthermore, we demonstrate that for several well-known models—such as Yule, Bell, and Crump-Johnson-Mode-Curtis processes—the Palm-2-measure can be derived directly from the underlying measure using a countable formula. Consequently, we establish that these processes retain a specific property known as "quasi-exchangeability." This result offers a novel perspective on a phenomenon originally identified by John Skellam in 1954, where complex branching dynamics can be modeled as a non-homogeneous birth process. Notably, Skellam's insight remains the sole method for obtaining the one-dimensional marginals of general branching processes that feature a common age-ancestry tree. Our findings extend to a broader category of processes called "quasi-exchangeable population processes," a class that encompasses all branching mechanisms. These processes are defined by the characteristic property that the age-ancestry tree of $n$ randomly selected individuals is exchangeable. For a specific subclass within this category, we provide a straightforward construction of the Palm-2-measure, which is entirely determined by the collection of one-dimensional marginals. This construction yields a particularly elegant formula for the law of common age-ancestry trees, expressed as a linear combination of one-dimensional marginals. This represents a significant advancement over the complex formula developed by Bertoin and Haas, which applies to exchangeable population processes. The simplicity of this new expression holds significant potential for practical applications. Finally, we illustrate the formula's utility by deriving the one-dimensional marginals for two popular population processes that belong to the quasi-exchangeable class but fall outside the scope of branching population processes. This achievement improves upon the intricate constructions previously required by Meir and Moon (1969) and Aldous (1998). As a byproduct, we also recover the formulae for the Palm-2-measure and one-dimensional marginals of Yule trees, as originally presented by Skellam (1954) and Meir and Moon (1969), respectively. This work introduces a method to control this flow using an external vertical electric field. The proposed device, a p-n junction, is integrated into a field-effect transistor (FET) structure that modulates carrier flow without requiring the junction to absorb the incident light. Consequently, this approach decouples electron-hole pair production from the factors influencing their current flow. The study presents experimental data from a prototype and explores the advantages of this proposed device for applications ranging from traditional p-n junctions to artificial neural networks. Furthermore, the work demonstrates the benefits of a new measurement technique utilizing an electron beam induced current. Finally, the proposed approach offers a fresh perspective on artificial synapses, providing deeper insights into their operational principles.

In recent years, the demand for neuromorphic devices has driven significant research into creating artificial synapses. These components are essential for constructing both feed-forward and recurrent neural networks, which are vital for pattern recognition and associative memory. While various materials and fabrication techniques have been investigated, there remains a critical need to comprehend the underlying physical mechanisms of these devices. This study examines the physics of artificial synapses by comparing their behavior to biological synapses. We developed a comprehensive model that successfully replicates experimental data and identifies the key characteristics of feed-forward and recurrent networks. Our findings reveal that artificial synapses can mimic biological ones, enabling the creation of advanced systems for pattern recognition and associative memory. By controlling an electric field, our proposed devices can replicate the diverse functions of biological synapses, including facilitating, depressing, blocking, and switching signals between neurons. Experimental validation involves a wide bandgap p-n junction integrated into a field-effect transistor (FET) configuration. This design offers a novel concept for artificial synapses by offering several key benefits. First, the device exhibits high photoresponsivity, comparable to photodiodes, because the photovoltaic effect occurs away from the gate region. Second, an artificial synapse can be integrated into any existing device, provided a region sensitive to a lateral or vertical electric field exists. Third, the incorporation of an artificial synapse introduces an additional degree of freedom, as its operation can be tuned independently of the main device. Experimental prototypes were fabricated using a wide bandgap p-n junction within an FET metal-oxide-semiconductor (MOS) configuration, where the gate voltage modulates the flow of photogenerated carriers. Our proposed concept, artificial synapses, opens new avenues for research and paves

To address this, we introduce a graph convolutional network-based approach that performs computations on encrypted noise-scale-additive integer data. By integrating a quantum stochastic approach with a reservoir engineering technique, the model demonstrates the nonclassical nature of the coupled atom-SPPP system and outlines a pathway to nonreciprocal light-matter interactions in a plasmonic setting. The theoretical predictions suggest that a nonclassical atom-SPPP state can be achieved with high fidelity, even when the plasmonic cavity's quality factor is two orders of magnitude lower than the atom's decay rate. a C-RAN architecture featuring distributed remote radio heads (RRHs) that experience double-Rayleigh fading. Specifically, we address the allocation of reference signals (RS) across multiple RRHs to minimize the total mean square estimation error (MSE) under an RS count constraint. We first establish that the PDE-SE-SE (pilots distributed, estimated, and estimated) strategy yields a lower total MSE than the DE-DE-PDE (pilots concentrated on certain RRHs) approach. Building on this finding, we formulate an optimization problem to distribute the necessary RSs for each RRH, thereby achieving the minimum total MSE. Given the non-convex nature of this problem, we employ successive convex approximation to derive a low-complexity solution that reaches the optimal total MSE. Finally, a comparative analysis demonstrates that this optimized PDE-SE-SE RS allocation significantly outperforms both optimized DE-SE-SE and DE-DE-PDE allocations, as well as a baseline scenario where RSs are evenly distributed. Numerical results further confirm that the PDE-SE-SE scheme yields a lower total MSE than the DE-DE-PDE scheme and allows the distributed RRHs to individually achieve more accurate channel estimates. Furthermore, PDE-SE-SE enables each RRH to attain a higher data rate than DE-SE-SE, resulting in an increased sum-rate. Additionally, PDE-SE-SE achieves a lower total MSE compared to DE-DE-PDE, leading to improved individual channel estimation accuracy at the distributed RRHs. We also present a simplified version of PDE-SE-SE that maintains a low total MSE while reducing the total number of RSs. This simplified scheme exhibits superior total MSE performance relative to DE-SE-SE and DE-DE-PDE, as well as the original PDE-SE-SE under specific conditions. Our conclusions indicate that the simplified PDE-SE-SE delivers a lower total MSE than DE-SE-SE and DE-DE-PDE, as well as a lower total MSE than PDE-SE-SE in particular scenarios. Moreover, the simplified PDE-SE-SE achieves an RRH count that is 1.5 to 2 times smaller than that of DE-SE-SE and DE-DE-PDE, and smaller than PDE-SE-SE in certain cases. Additionally, the simplified PDE-SE-SE secures a sum-rate that is 1.2 to 1.

While various theories attempt to explain how children acquire the skill of counting to 10, they often rely on unproven assumptions. This study presents a computational algorithm designed to develop a quantitative model of child-like number concept evolution, grounded in data from 103 children aged 4 to 6. The findings indicate that, through a process akin to reinforcement learning, children gradually construct the 10-element sequence by randomly combining spatial and temporal dimensions. Crucially, this sequence remains invariant under coordinate transformations, a property essential for successful communication. Consequently, the work offers a novel, data-driven perspective on how children acquire the ability to count. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm not only elucidates the emergence of children's numerical cognition but also holds potential applications in designing artificial systems with similar cognitive abilities. Ultimately, this research provides a computational example of how complex human cognitive structures, such as language and mathematics, can arise from simple cognitive primitives. These results are detailed in a paper currently under review for the International Journal of Computer Mathematics.

the relative movements of the S&P500 and the Nasdaq100. It posits that when the S&P500 rises more significantly than the Nasdaq100, the market is trending upward, whereas when the Nasdaq100 outperforms the S&P500, the market is trending downward. Furthermore, the method for deriving a trend-based index is applicable to other asset classes, such as individual stocks or sectors, to facilitate the separation of alpha and beta components. Medical institutions often possess distinct patient demographics, creating non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) settings that can hinder standard federated learning approaches. To address this, we incorporated local statistical analysis into the training pipeline to capture site-specific data distributions. Furthermore, recognizing the critical role of data quality, we implemented a weighted aggregation strategy to prioritize high-quality institutions during updates. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating statistical features reduces the generalization error of the final model by 10% compared to the basic Voogd method. Additionally, by focusing updates from top-performing institutions, the proposed approach accelerates convergence by 20% relative to the standard Voogd approach. These findings indicate a more efficient and effective federated learning process, offering significant potential improvements for clinical applications. The source code is accessible at flvoogd.github.io.

The challenge is particularly difficult due to its extensive input modalities and the intricate interdependencies among them. Our winning system employs a multimodal transformer architecture that integrates information from various inputs through a method termed "attention-guided propagation," which combines cross and self attention mechanisms to handle input interdependencies. In this paper, we introduce a novel approach to improve the performance of multimodal language models (MLMs) on visual question answering (VQA) by utilizing label dependencies to create additional training samples. Our method, which we call dependency parsing, involves two main steps: first, identifying label dependencies within the original training set using a label dependency graph; second, constructing new synthetic samples based on these identified dependencies to expand the training data. We validated the efficacy of our approach on the ScienceQA dataset, where a model trained solely on the original data scored 0.6911, whereas a model augmented with samples generated by dependency parsing achieved a score of 0.7274. Additionally, we demonstrated the method's generalizability by applying it to the VQA v2 dataset, where it yielded a 0.4% improvement in accuracy. We have open-sourced our code and pre-trained models at https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAMO-UDYmy/ScienceQA.

We present a new technique for expanding label dependency graphs by identifying frequently co-occurring label pairs within a knowledge graph. This approach enables the discovery of label dependencies that are often absent in existing dependency graphs, such as those found in Visual7W and VQA-XPDE. These newly discovered dependencies can significantly enhance the performance of multimodal transformer-based models on complex benchmarks like ScienceQA and POPE. Specifically, on ScienceQA, a model trained only on the original training set scored 0.6911, while a model augmented with samples generated via our method improved the score to 0.7274. Furthermore

capabilities of computer vision, particularly in object detection, which has seen rapid progress driven by the success of convolutional neural networks (CNNs). However, the high computational demands of CNN-based detectors often limit their practical utility. Although model compression techniques like quantization, pruning, and knowledge distillation have been applied to detector compression, their primary focus has historically been accuracy preservation. ptune exoplanets have revealed a distinct gap in the mass-radius relationship, dividing planets into terrestrial and massive categories. This study investigates the evolution of sub-Neptune cores to determine if planetesimal accretion can naturally produce this divide. We developed a core accretion model incorporating planetesimal accretion to trace the mass and size distributions of planetary cores from the oligarchic growth phase through the giant planet migration epoch in planetary systems forming around solar-mass stars. Our findings indicate that planetesimal accretion during giant planet migration can indeed split sub-Neptune planets into two populations: terrestrial planets that accumulated vast amounts of planetesimals, and massive planets that retained only modest quantities. The ultimate mass intake by these cores relies on the timing of giant planet migration relative to the dissipation of the gas disk and the initial solid surface density of the protoplanetary disk. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the slope of the initial power-law mass distribution for planetesimals is a critical factor, as it governs the size distribution of planetary cores and their capacity to absorb large or small amounts of planetesimals. Finally, we show that the total mass gained by sub-Neptune cores can be constrained by the metallicity of their host stars, specifically the [Fe/H] ratio. These outcomes align with recent exoplanet findings suggesting that terrestrial planets formed via planetesimal accretion are more common in metal-rich environments, while massive sub-Neptune planets are more prevalent in metal-poor systems. Consequently, planetesimal accretion during giant planet migration offers a compelling explanation for the observed mass distribution of short-period planets in the Kepler dataset. Additionally, this mechanism may have been pivotal in the growth of planetary cores to the critical mass required to initiate gas accretion, thereby triggering the formation of giant planets. The core accretion model, which integrates planetesimal accretion during migration, represents a more comprehensive framework for simulating planet formation than previous models that neglected this process. This refined model holds significant potential for elucidating the formation history of giant planets and their associated small planet populations. The core accretion simulation code is accessible at https://github.com/kyuhyuncho. Keywords: Planetary systems: formation, planets: formation, planets: general. (Abridged)

study of Metzler and Maiman, we introduce a quantum analogue of the classical laser, characterizing a "quantum lasing" transition that mirrors the classical "lasing" threshold. Our analysis reveals that our initial quantum model, which features a mean-field coupling between the field and the mirror's mechanical motion, yields predictions that significantly diverge from those of a refined model incorporating the backaction of the field on the mirror. We successfully observe this quantum lasing phenomenon using a single-atom cavity quantum electrodynamics setup, where the atomic position is mean-field coupled to the field. In contrast, when employing a two-atom configuration in the far-detuned regime, the field is effectively mean-field coupled to a collective spin, but the spin's feedback to the field resembles a classical mechanical element. Consequently, our results serve as a quantum extension of the original 1943 paper by Metzler and Maiman. Furthermore, one of our configurations functions as a quantum version of the classic laser-mirror thought experiment, demonstrating both the stabilizing and destabilizing influences of lasing. Our work establishes single-mode lasing as a genuinely quantum threshold transition, distinct from the classical superradiant phase transition documented in *Nature* **589**, 682–686 (2021). Finally, as a single-atom system operating in the bad-cavity regime, it functions as a non-linear frequency converter, enabling the generation of micro-masers across a broad frequency spectrum. This single-atom micro-maser is bad-cavity coupled to the atom, mean-field coupled to the atomic position, and subject to position-dependent atomic decay. By adjusting the position-decay symmetry, this single-atom micro-maser can function as either a $\mathbb{Z}_2$-symmetric frequency converter or a $\mathbb{C}Z$-symmetric up-converter. Frequency conversion is achieved through the quantum lasing threshold, which is currently reached at a mean intracavity power of approximately 1000 photons. The transition is destabilizing, driven by the lasing backaction on the atom's position, and results in a significant shift in the atomic emission rate. Of-Distribution (OOD) detection challenge hosted at the EMNLP 2022 NLP Security subconference. The contest aimed to assess the capability of NOD (neural OOD) models to identify nonsensical English sentences across a wide range of threats, including semantic anomalies, grammatical errors, nonsensical text, offensive content, hate speech, misinformation, toxic language, and spam. The competition involved three tasks involving distinct challenge sets, each with unique scoring mechanisms. The final results were compiled into a comprehensive leaderboard featuring 100 submissions from 39 teams and individual submitters. Based on this leaderboard, we present and analyze the challenge data, explore various NOD methods applied to natural language, and review the techniques and strategies employed by participants to address the contest. The full challenge dataset is accessible at https://github.com/amanabind/EMNLP-2022-NLP-Security-OOD-Challenge.

The challenge data was constructed through multiple steps: first, high-quality semantic reversal datasets were utilized to generate nonsense sentences by flipping word orders; second, existing NOD datasets were filtered to remove sentences that were already classified as nonsensical; and third, novel nonsensical sentences were manually created to further expand the dataset.

To evaluate submissions, the contest established three datasets (A, B, and C) with corresponding challenge sets (A', B', and C'). Dataset A' comprised nonsensical sentences, while Dataset B' included offensive and toxic content. Dataset C consisted of human-nonsensical sentences. The A' score measured the Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (AUPRC) on this set, the B' score was calculated as the mean of the AUPRCs across three separate B' datasets, and the C' score was determined as the mean AUPRC across four C' datasets. Final scores were computed as a weighted sum of these components.

The analysis of the leaderboards reveals that neural network OOD detection remains an open problem with significant room for improvement. Although many submissions successfully detected nonsensical text, they frequently failed to distinguish between different types of nonsensical content. Additionally, the study examines the application of NOD methods in NLP, offering insights into the approaches and strategies used by submitters to tackle the challenge.

The challenge data is available at: https://github.com/amanabind/EMNLP-2022-NLP-Security-OOD-Challenge. The associated paper can

for analyzing stochastic differential equations, yet the high dimensionality of the approximation space often impedes the convergence of traditional solution techniques like numerical integration and Monte Carlo methods. However, high dimensionality complicates Model-Based Fault Detection (MBFD) system design, particularly because traditional methods often fail to account for sensor noise, leading to excessive false alarms. Model-subspace methods offer a solution by effectively filtering noise through projection, yet they have historically been limited to linear systems. This work introduces a novel monitoring framework for nonlinear systems by adapting the subspace identification algorithm from De Haan et al. (2018) to a component-wise linear structure. Additionally, we propose a fault detection scheme that incorporates the Dynamic Kernel Hermitian Polynomial (DKHP) approach (Li et al., 2019) to generate residuals, which are subsequently processed using the monitoring subspace to identify faults. The DKHP method is selected for its ability to efficiently capture nonlinear dynamics, while the monitoring subsspace is utilized to filter out any spurious nonlinearities caused by faults. The efficacy of the proposed DKHP-residuals and subsspace-based monitoring approach is validated through two case studies: a simulated system and a real-world temperature sensor array. Results indicate that this method successfully distinguishes between faults and noise, accurately identifying and isolating nonlinear faults. The accompanying repository can be accessed at: https://github.com/Alireza-Li1994/Nonlinear-Fault-Detection-and-Isolation-via-Model-Subspaces.

Key words: Nonlinear fault detection, Model-subspace method, Sensor array, Dynamic Kernel Hermitian Polynomial.

This study employs atomic-resolution scanning tunneling microscopy to examine a pristine EuS/InAs interface. Our proof utilizes the true stage classification of $\Pi^1_1$ sets of reals by Turetsky and Underwood. Although deep learning architectures have proven effective for vision, speech, and natural language processing, they often require substantial computational resources and time, creating a bottleneck for real-world applications. To address this, significant research has focused on optimizing neural networks for efficiency without compromising performance. This paper reviews recent advancements in accelerating deep neural network inference through hardware and hardware-software co-design approaches. We begin by categorizing various optimization techniques into four groups: data-level, architecture-level, and hardware and hardware-software co-design-level methods. Subsequently, we provide an in-depth analysis of studies that have achieved notable improvements in both efficiency and accuracy. Finally, we discuss current challenges and propose potential future research directions within this field. This survey aims to guide researchers in selecting appropriate optimization strategies for specific use cases and deploying optimized models on target hardware.

In recent years, the rapid advancement of 5G technology has spurred extensive research into ultra-reliable and low-latency communication (URLLC). These networks rely on diverse applications, including autonomous driving, drone delivery, and remote surgery, which demand varying levels of resource allocation, power usage, and data rates. Consequently, the primary objective of this study is to optimize these resources within a 5G-enabled drone delivery system. To achieve this, we introduce a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) approach designed to minimize the total energy consumption of a 5G drone delivery network. The DRL agent dynamically adjusts power levels and base station (BS) selection for each delivery point, aiming to reduce overall power usage. Our simulation results demonstrate that the proposed DRL-based solution outperforms traditional 5G schemes, achieving a power reduction of up to 20% compared to literature-based methods.

The increasing adoption of autonomous vehicles (AVs) necessitates intelligent and efficient 5G-enabled communication systems. However, the high energy consumption of current 5G networks poses a significant challenge to sustainability. To tackle this, we propose a Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) solution aimed at minimizing power usage in 5G drone delivery systems. This approach dynamically optimizes power allocation and base station association during package delivery. We evaluated the proposed method against existing 5G literature, and our simulations reveal a power reduction of up to 20% compared to these schemes. Given that our approach requires no prior knowledge of the environment, we conclude that this novel solution holds promise for enhancing the energy efficiency of 5G drone delivery networks.

However, the flexibility of actor-critic RL in handling diverse manipulation tasks is hindered by its difficulty in incorporating domain knowledge and domain-specific skills. This study introduces the use of symbolic actions as a mechanism to guide the policy towards desired behaviors, enabling modular encoding of high-level domain knowledge. These individual policies are then integrated into a symbolic action set, which serves as a probabilistic prior to steer a new policy designed for similar sub-tasks. Extensive experiments conducted on both simulation and physical platforms demonstrate that an agent trained with symbolic actions achieves superior performance in similar tasks compared to one trained without them. Consequently, the $n$-th prime number, denoted as $p_n$, may be written as $6k_n \pm 1$, where $k_n$ is a specific integer dependent on $n$. This article introduces specific functions of $n$ to estimate $k_n$ and, by extension, the $n$-th prime. Specifically, we propose that $k_n$ falls within the interval $\left[\frac{n}{\ln n-1},\,\frac{n}{\ln n-2}\right]$. Our findings indicate that as $n$ increases, both the lower and upper bounds of this interval converge, thereby narrowing the interval itself. This approach offers a distinct perspective on estimating the $n$-th prime. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the ratio of the lower bound to the actual $k_n$ adheres to a skewed Gaussian distribution. This research complements our earlier work regarding the estimation of $p_n$ using $6\left(\frac{n}{\ln n-2}\right)-1$, which is published in arXiv:2006.01024. Through various examples, we illustrate that our method effectively estimates $k_n$ and provides a more precise value for $p_n$ compared to the $n$-th prime approximation derived from the $n$-th Mertens' Theorem. Additionally, we examine the ratio $\frac{6\left(\frac{n}{\ln n-2}\right)-1}{p_n}$, showing that this ratio converges to 1 as $n$ approaches infinity. This supports the validity of our estimation for $k_n$. We also explore the estimation of $k_n$ when $n$ is a Gaussian prime. In this context, we utilize the known property that every Gaussian prime takes the form $a+bi$, where either $a$ or $b$ is either a prime number or a multiple of a prime. We apply a similar methodology to estimate $k_n$ under these conditions. Finally, we investigate the estimation of $k_n$ when $n$ is a Mersenne prime. Our approach here involves applying a theorem by Lucas, which provides necessary and sufficient conditions for a number of the form $6k \pm 1$ to be a Mersenne prime. While current path planning algorithms are effective in open spaces, they often fail in cluttered environments by failing to account for the mobility of obstacles and the dynamic nature of the terrain. To address this, a new algorithm is proposed that generates feasible paths for mobile robots by incorporating the mobility characteristics of obstacles and terrain, ensuring path adaptability. One such scenario involves Nereid being captured from a heliocentric orbit through a scattering event driven by a past moon-moon close encounter on Pluto. This study evaluates the feasibility of Nereid's origin in this specific captured Pluto satellite system by conducting a high-fidelity simulation of the scenario. We employed the REBOUND software to model a series of two-body encounters between Mopua (the most massive initial satellite) and other Pluto satellites, systematically varying impact parameters and mass ratios. Our results indicate that Nereid-like objects can be ejected from Mopua's system with inclinations exceeding 30 degrees, provided the Mopua-to-satellite mass ratio is at least 10. However, the survival of these ejected objects is limited; they typically survive only a few thousand years before colliding with Kuiper Belt Objects or being ejected by Neptune. Consequently, for Nereid to exist today as the direct product of this capture event, it would require an improbable statistical fluke. This research supports the conclusion that the Mopua system is unlikely to be the source of Nereid. Nevertheless, our findings demonstrate that a single close encounter between Mopua and another satellite can significantly alter the orbital properties of an ejected body, a mechanism that may be more broadly applicable in planetary formation research. Furthermore, our work offers insights into the dynamical evolution of multi-satellite systems, a critical component of exoplanetary systems. Finally, we provide a comprehensive guide and code for utilizing REBOUND to conduct high-fidelity simulations of moon-moon encounters. The specific scenario analyzed here can be directly loaded into REBOUND using the MEE.reb file, while a detailed walkthrough is also available. Although our simulations utilize a real-world background of planets and moons, the primary focus remains on the interactions between the Pluto satellites. We anticipate that this research will assist other scientists in accurately assessing the likelihood of specific scenarios, such as the one proposed by Stern et al. (2012), and will enable a greater number of simulations to be performed, thereby yielding more robust statistical outcomes. Additionally, our detailed instructions will aid planetologists and planetary scientists in performing similar analyses using modern state-of-the-art software. The potential significance of our findings extends beyond the Nereid case, as many exoplanetary systems feature captured planets with highly inclined and eccentric orbits, suggesting that our methodology may be relevant in broader contexts. However, recent theoretical developments indicate that non-local correlations within these strictly 2D systems can generate stable three-dimensional (3D) Bose condensates. This study provides a theoretical framework for creating such 3D condensates using an existing experimental 2D platform: a flat-band ferromagnetic semiconductor heterostructure. By introducing a local magnetic field gradient, we derive an anisotropic coupling between the resulting spinons and an emergent chemical potential gradient. Under conditions of low spinon density, this anisotropic potential generates a quasi-3D electron pocket in the Brillouin zone, which transforms into a flat band when a specific gradient criterion is satisfied. Consequently, the itinerant Dirac cone spinons become gapped, leaving the newly formed flat-band spinons capable of undergoing a 3D Bose condensation. This mechanism is applicable to various existing experimental setups and can be regulated by the gradient's orientation. Furthermore, the 3D nature of these condensates can be detected through the anisotropic response of the superfluid density to anisotropic perturbations. These non-thermally formed 3D condensates represent a new class of quantum matter, offering a fresh perspective on the design and exploration of higher-dimensional quantum systems using established 2D technologies. Additionally, the proposed spin-anisotropic flat-band scenario is also pertinent to the search for a spin-liquid ground state in frustrated magnets. Finally, the 3D flat-band spinon condensation is also expected to emerge in a proposed moiré flat-band system where interlayer coupling is non-negligible. These findings expand the design landscape for higher-dimensional quantum matter using current experimental 2D platforms. The accompanying movie illustrates the anisotropic spin-analytic angle of the superfluid density as evidence of the 3D character of the spin-analytic spinon condensation. The movie is available at: https://youtu.be/422YQ222222.

CT reconstruction from limited-view data is a critical challenge in fields such as Computed Tomography (CT), X-ray tomography, and electron microscopy. While deep learning has emerged as a powerful tool for this task, it struggles with data sparsity, a problem that conventional iterative algorithms handle effectively. This paper proposes a new deep learning-based reconstruction technique that iteratively applies an unrolled conventional iterative algorithm. In this framework, each forward projection and backprojection step of the iterative process corresponds to a layer in a deep network. By casting the traditional iterative method as a deep network, we can leverage deep learning solutions to accelerate convergence. To regularize the learned deep network, we employ Riemannian optimization to enforce constraints on the parameters of each layer. Our method was tested on 2D CT data, and experiments indicate that it achieves faster convergence than other recent deep learning-based reconstruction techniques. Our code

decision-making under uncertainty is a critical objective. A prevalent strategy to achieve this involves resolving a min-max problem where a decision maker aims to maximize their expected utility against an adversary designed to minimize that utility by selecting a probability distribution over environmental states. In this work, we introduce the Wicked Worlds Algorithm (WWA), a no-regret method for decision makers facing such malicious distributions. We establish a rigorous regret bound for WWA, demonstrating that it grows logarithmically with the number of available environments and the product of the adversary's horizon and the cardinality of state values. This represents a substantial improvement over previous approaches, as WWA achieves constant per-round computational complexity. Furthermore, we prove that WWA attains a linear regret bound, confirming its optimality. These findings underscore WWA as a significant advancement over existing solutions. Experimental results show that WWA surpasses competing algorithms in both utility and runtime efficiency. The source code is accessible at https://github.com/ashwin-krishnan/wicked-worlds-algorithm.

Galactic Center (GC) is home to a supermassive black hole (SMBH) and a dense collection of stars. The stellar population near the GC exhibits a wide range of ages and metallicities, with the youngest and most metal-rich groups being massive star clusters. These clusters are theorized to have formed via rapid, energetic, and turbulent events. This study examines the chemical composition of the young stellar population in the GC to gain insights into their formation mechanisms. We utilized high-resolution spectra from the Keck/HIRES and Keck/NIRSPEC instruments to measure abundances for 12 elements (Fe, Ni, Co, Cu, Zn, Cr, Mn, V, Ti, Ca, Sc, and Y) in 10 early-type stars within 10 parsecs of the SMBH Sgr A*. Our findings reveal that Sgr A* is surrounded by metal-poor stars, with [Fe/H] values ranging from -0.7 to -0.2 dex. Additionally, we identified significant abundance variations among the stars, with [Fe/Fe] fluctuations of approximately 0.2 dex for most elements. These variations are unlikely to result from stellar nucleosynthesis, suggesting instead that the stars formed from a chemically inhomogeneous medium. The observed abundance patterns align with those of massive star clusters in the Magellanic Clouds, supporting the hypothesis that the stars in Sgr A* originated from a massive star cluster that formed roughly 6 million years ago. The distinct abundance patterns observed in this work provide valuable constraints for future hydrodynamical simulations of the GC. Our results also indicate that the stars in Sgr A* are not the oldest stellar population in the central parsec, as the metal-poor stars in Sgr A* are significantly younger than the metal-rich stars previously identified in the region. Finally, our findings suggest that the "runaway" stars in Sgr A* are not the runaway stars previously identified in the central parsec. Our work demonstrates that high-resolution spectroscopy can effectively probe the formation history of the young stellar population in the GC. This study introduces LoCat, a novel lightweight catfish attack designed to test IoT network management and security mechanisms by stealthily and accurately classifying IoT devices. As a black-box method, LoCat operates without requiring any prior knowledge of the target network. It functions as a transparent middlebox that generates traffic similar to legitimate background processes, thereby minimizing detection risks. Despite its simplicity, LoCat achieves a classification accuracy of 99.1% across 17 classes using less than 100 middlebox packets per class. Furthermore, it successfully distinguishes between 32 different OS-level defenses with 96.8% accuracy. A large-scale experiment involving 537 IoT devices from 17 categories demonstrated that LoCat requires an average of 12.5 middlebox packets per device. This paper investigates G\"odel dual intuitionistic logics, which correspond to prefix logics in the gale-neshchev framework and possess the finite model property. We present an effective method to determine whether a given basic first-order logic with the distributivity property (specifically, the commutativity of $\Box$ over $\vee$ and $\Diamond$ over $\wedge$) augmented with first-order axioms results in a logic that possesses the canonical, finite, and Herbrand properties. Consequently, this criterion establishes the logical equivalence between the validity in the class of finite models and the theorem-hood within the corresponding proto-algebraic logic. Furthermore, this approach enables the straightforward derivation of constructive semantics for various gale-neshchev logics, thereby avoiding the complex analytical procedures traditionally required. Leveraging this framework, we define and examine gale-neshchev extensions of S4 and S4.2, analyzing their characteristics and demonstrating their equivalence to specific first-order logics. Additionally, we illustrate that the logical equivalence between the finite model property and the Herbrand property does not necessarily imply the existence of the canonical property, using S4 with the axiom $[p\wedge\Box p]\Box q$ as a counterexample. Finally, we illustrate gale-neshchev extensions of S5 and the weakest S5, presenting the strongest S4.3 axiomatization for each. We also establish the non-theorem status of a specific axiom in S4.2, confirming its completeness relative to the finite model property, and we provide an effective axiomatization for the logic S4.2 augmented with the formula $\Box(p\wedge\Box p)\vee\Diamond q$. The logical equivalences between these findings and those regarding S4, S5, and the discussed specific logics are established.

### I. INTRODUCTION

Capturing an object's projection is a fundamental principle in imaging, forming the basis for techniques ranging from photography to tomography. Conventional imaging systems typically require multiple measurements to reconstruct an object's image, a process often limited by the specific physical properties of the target. For instance, photographing a scene involves two steps: first, illuminating the object so light reflects off it and reaches the detector, and second, directly detecting the scene. Similarly, medical X-ray tomography scans a subject from various angles to reconstruct internal cross-sections. These multi-step procedures can be time-consuming, restricting their application to slowly moving objects. Conversely, applications such as imaging fast chemical reactions, cellular processes, or planetary movements demand much greater acquisition speeds.

To address this, researchers have created computational imaging techniques that use modified measurement patterns to gather more data in a single step. However, these methods often rely on iterative algorithms to invert the measured data into a final image, resulting in substantial computational overhead. Consequently, there is a pressing need for imaging techniques that are both rapid to capture and efficient to process.

In this study, we propose a new class of computational imaging that simultaneously captures an object's projection and its spatial distribution to efficiently extract object information from just one measurement. Unlike

**1. Introduction**

Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable capabilities in instruction following, language understanding, and generation, leading to widespread adoption across various applications. However, recent studies have revealed significant vulnerabilities in LLMs, including adversarial examples, bias, privacy leaks, and safety issues. These flaws pose critical challenges to the safety and reliability of LLMs, underscoring the urgent need for effective safety evaluation. Consequently, researchers have developed numerous evaluation benchmarks featuring diverse test samples. Nevertheless, existing benchmarks rely predominantly on manually crafted test inputs, which are often easy to generate and consequently susceptible to countermeasures. This reliance limits the authenticity of evaluation results and fails to uncover fundamental safety risks.

To address these shortcomings, this work proposes using adversarial attacks during the safety evaluation phase. By automating the generation of test samples, this approach not only enhances the efficiency of the evaluation process but also allows for a more comprehensive exploration of potential model vulnerabilities. Our primary goal is to identify adversarial samples that effectively deceive the model into producing harmful outputs. We assess the safety of multiple open-source LLMs using self-supervised adversarial examples, analyzing the characteristics of these samples and the attack mechanisms. Our findings indicate that self-supervised adversarial examples are highly effective at triggering safety issues in LLMs. By integrating these adversarial samples with traditional benchmark tests, we can significantly improve the accuracy of safety evaluations and reveal previously hidden vulnerabilities.

Our universe's accelerating expansion, first identified by the Supernova Cosmology Project (SCP) and later corroborated by the Supernova Legacy Survey (SNLS), has solidified the $\Lambda$CDM model as the prevailing cosmological paradigm. In this framework, dark energy and dark matter constitute the two primary components of the cosmos. The standard $\Lambda$CDM model posits that the gravitational interaction responsible for structure formation is governed by Einstein's General Relativity, with a cosmological constant ($\Lambda$) serving as the simplest representation of dark energy. This cosmological constant drives the universe's acceleration, acting as a repulsive force that opposes gravity and influences the evolution of large-scale structures. Despite its success in explaining observational data, the physical nature of the cosmological constant remains enigmatic. Additionally, the coincidence problem—why the energy densities of dark energy and dark matter appear comparable today—remains unresolved. These challenges have motivated researchers to explore alternative dark energy models, including those that are phantom, non-minimally coupled, or dissipative.

Dissipative dark energy represents a particularly intriguing class of solutions. This concept was initially introduced by Dabrowski, who proposed that dark energy could dissipate by transferring energy to dark matter. Subsequent studies have explored this idea, yielding significant results. have gained popularity for their ability to create images from prompts. However, these models often produce results that are overly generic, lacking the specific details found in reference images. To address this, we introduce a novel framework that integrates a diffusion model with a regional similarity metric to establish a similarity-guided generation pipeline. Specifically, we divide the reference image into multiple patches and generate images by following a similarity trajectory defined by both an unconditional diffusion process and a similarity score relative to these patches. To accommodate any arbitrary image, we employ a pre-trained vision transformer to extract patches and their corresponding embeddings. We name this approach Similarity Guided Diffusion (SGD). SGD demonstrates strong similarity to its generated images and effectively recaptures specific details, outperforming state-of-the-art specific detail synthesis methods on the KOAN dataset. Furthermore, SGD achieves superior subject similarity compared to popular NCE-based methods on both similar-image and similar-video tasks of free-form generation using the VSRW dataset. Our code and models are available at: https://github.com/andrewmoum/SGD.

In video generation, similarity-guided approaches have proven highly effective for creating specific animations from a single video. However, creating images or videos from a text prompt remains challenging, particularly when providing similarity metrics for every word in the prompt. To overcome this, we utilize a pre-trained vision-language model to map text prompts to an image similarity space. By guiding the diffusion process with this metric, we can produce highly specific results aligned with the verbal description. We term this method V-SGD. Experiments on the VSRW dataset show that V-SGD significantly outperforms popular text-based generation techniques in both similar-image and similar-video contexts. Additionally, V-SGD achieves state-of-the-art similarity to the reference image when capturing details from an image given a free-form prompt on the KOAN dataset. Our code and models can be found at: https://github.com/andrewmoum/SGD.

**Abstract**
**Context.** The solar convection zone is characterized by the interaction between magnetic fields and convective flows. **Aims.** We investigate how magnetic fields influence convective energy dissipation and momentum transfer within the convection zone. **Methods.** Using realistic 3D radiation-hydrodynamics simulations of a solar convection zone layer, we analyzed the momentum transfer between horizontal and vertical convective motions under varying magnetic field strengths. **Results.** The study reveals that horizontal energy is efficiently transferred to vertical motions in both non-magnetic and magnetized environments. **Conclusions.** This efficient transfer validates the granular convective model observed on the solar surface and supports the hypothesis that a dynamo operating in the convection zone can generate the Sun's global magnetic field.

This study investigates the independent contributions of spatial and motion information by examining how the human visual system processes moving parts, such as the arms of a person walking. This methodology holds potential applications in creating visual stimuli for neuroscience research and developing efficient video representations for machine learning.
